The search found useful sources, though not much formal research. Most of the criticism comes from developer blogs and GitHub discussions, and nothing specifically about WCAG turned up.

**Main criticisms of hold-to-confirm:**
- **Keyboard access:** The most common failure in a "hold to confirm" is that it only works with the mouse, which makes the destructive action unreachable for keyboard users. The same GitHub issue says the pattern needs a visible progress indicator, a cancel-on-release/release-path, keyboard support (holding Enter/Space), and the same server-side effect as a click — because a UI delay isn't a security control, it's a friction control.
- **Hard to discover, no sense of duration:** In a React implementation post, Dzialowski notes that the user isn't sure how much longer they need to keep holding the button and that users might not immediately grasp that holding the button is necessary instead of just clicking it. He suggests a popover that appears when the user clicks (but doesn't hold) the button. He also says ensuring that this button remains user-friendly for keyboard interactions is not a straightforward task. His advice is to reserve the use of the "hold to confirm" approach for exceptional cases.

**The argument in favor (DEV Community, Tom J):**
- He describes the mechanism: a visual indicator (like a progress bar) fills up over the hold period. If the user releases the button before completion, the action is canceled. He recommends that if the button is clicked (not held), a brief movement of the progress bar signals that the user should hold the button. His team now uses it by default for any action that changes the state of an item.

**Alternatives and general guidance for destructive actions:**
- **Undo first, then typed confirmation:** Ideally, we should allow users to undo destructive actions. If an undo button cannot be implemented, we can prompt users to type the destructive action in a text field to confirm
- **Where focus lands:** Dropping focus directly onto the confirm button invites accidental activation by someone who pressed Enter out of habit. Also, the Escape key should dismiss it, a visible Cancel control should be present, and dismissing it must never trigger the destructive action.
- **Dialog accessibility:** focus trapping, Esc to cancel, return focus to the trigger, aria-modal/aria-labelledby/aria-describedby.
- **Overuse and color:** Using confirmatory dialogs for routine actions can affect the way users perceive destructive action dialogs. In addition, relying on colour alone is not appropriate due to accessibility and cultural differences.
- **Smashing Magazine (2024)** covers modal dialogs, typing "DELETE" to confirm, and the "Danger zone" pattern.

**Gaps:** None of the results ties hold-to-confirm to specific WCAG criteria, such as 2.5.1 (Pointer Gestures), 2.1.1 (Keyboard), or the timing criteria. None covers screen reader announcement of hold progress or motor impairments like tremor. Searches like "WCAG long press" or "press and hold motor impairment accessibility" might fill those gaps.

The search turned up Apple's official HIG Motion page (both the current `.md` version and an older Foundations URL). It confirms the guidelines you were looking for:

**Current HIG Motion page (developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion):**
- Purpose: "Add motion purposefully, supporting the experience without overshadowing it. Don't add motion for the sake of adding motion."
- Optional motion: "Make motion optional. Not everyone can or wants to experience the motion in your app or game, so it's essential to avoid using it as the only way to communicate important information."
- Brevity: "Aim for brevity and precision in feedback animations. When animated feedback is brief and precise, it tends to feel lightweight and unobtrusive, and it can often convey information more effectively than prominent animation."
- Frequent interactions: "In apps, generally avoid adding motion to UI interactions that occur frequently. The system already provides subtle animations for interactions with standard interface elements." "For a custom element, you generally want to avoid making people spend extra time paying attention to unnecessary motion every time they interact with it."
- Intro: "System components might also adjust their motion in response to factors like accessibility settings or different input methods."

**Older wording (developers.apple.com/.../foundations/motion):** The frequent-interactions rule used to say "In general, avoid adding motion to interactions that occur frequently." and "Avoid making people spend extra time watching unnecessary motion every time they interact with something." The realism rule was worded as "Strive for realism and credibility." If you cite the guidelines, use the current page's wording.

**Supporting details:**
- The Use Your Loaf blog quotes the HIG line: "Gratuitous or excessive animation can distract people and may make them feel disconnected or physically uncomfortable."
- It also lists motions Apple flags as risky, including "Oscillating motions, especially with large amplitudes and frequencies around 0.2 Hz (one oscillation every five seconds)." This could matter for the endless `gentle-pulse` animation.

**Not in these results:** The "Let people cancel motion" rule and the current "realistic feedback motion" wording that you quoted earlier don't appear in these snippets, so this search doesn't confirm them. The snippets are partial, so those lines may still be on the full page. The official page also doesn't use the phrase "Reduce Motion"; that term only shows up in third-party sources like Uxcel.

I couldn't find a tutorial built specifically around a procedural paper shader with grain and fibre in three.js. What came back was mostly general normal-mapping guides. The closest is the Tips4Devs article, which actually uses a paper texture.

**Most relevant results**
- **[Tips4Devs: Create a Photo Normal Map for Three.js](https://tips4devs.com/articles/create-a-photo-normal-map-for-threejs.html)** (2019): creates a volume effect by overlapping several images taken at different light directions. The resulting `MeshPhongMaterial` uses a `paperTexture` as its map. The render-target texture is used as both its `specularMap` and `normalMap`, with a `PointLight` lighting it.
- **[ilovesprites: PBR Textures in Three.js](https://ilovesprites.com/blog/threejs-pbr-textures-normal-maps)** (about 4 months old): the practical points that matter for a paper surface.
  - Tag the color map as `SRGBColorSpace`, but leave the normal map untagged because it's data, not color.
  - Start `normalScale` at 1 and adjust it by eye with the light moving.
  - Its pipeline: make it tileable in the Seamless Texture tool, feed that result to the Normal Map Generator (the seamless version, so the normal map tiles too).
- **[Medium: Advanced Texture Mapping in Three.js](https://medium.com/@sohail_saifi/advanced-texture-mapping-in-three-js-make-your-3d-models-stand-out-18577bb3322b)**: uses `onBeforeCompile` to add a second normal map after `#include <normal_fragment_maps>`. It blends the two with `normalize(vec3(n1.xy + n2.xy, n1.z * n2.z))`. That's handy for stacking fine grain on top of a larger fibre or crinkle layer.
- **[Dustin Pfister: Making a normal map in threejs](https://dustinpfister.github.io/2021/06/24/threejs-normal-map/)**: draws normal maps on a canvas and uses them as a `CanvasTexture` on a `MeshStandardMaterial`. You could use the same approach to generate fibre or grain normals in code.
- **[SBCode NormalMap tutorial](https://sbcode.net/threejs/normalmap/)**: the basic setup of `MeshPhongMaterial` with `normalMap`, `normalScale.set(2,2)` and a `PointLight`.
- **[three.js forum: grainy material due to normal map](https://discourse.threejs.org/t/distorted-grainy-material-due-to-a-normal-map/72599)**: a pitfall to avoid. UVs stretched along one axis cause normal-map artifacts. Set tiling with `texture.repeat` and `texture.offset` rather than changing the geometry.

**Gaps:** none of the results covers a fully procedural paper shader in GLSL or TSL, for example noise-based fibres, grain and paper-coloured diffuse lighting. Searches worth trying next: "procedural paper shader GLSL", "shadertoy paper texture", or "watercolor paper shader three.js".

Sources agree that feTurbulence is one of the most expensive SVG filter primitives. Its cost goes up with the number of octaves, the size of the area it covers and how often it updates. The most common fix is to swap a full-page noise filter for a static tiled image.

**Why it's slow:**
- One guide says feTurbulence gets easier to feel the cost as octaves, affected area, and update frequency grow. Small elements with restrained parameter ranges are far safer than large continuously animated surfaces.
- A Mozilla bug report notes that it gets slower as numOctaves increases; the default value is 1 (the reporter was using 9). In that bug, Firefox nearly froze when the window was maximized.
- One guide's cost table rates feTurbulence "Very heavy", feDisplacementMap "Heavy", feGaussianBlur "Heavy (radius dependent)" and feColorMatrix "Light". It also says chained filters add up. 
- Even though most modern browsers GPU-accelerate common filter primitives like feGaussianBlur, complex chains or very large filter regions can still fall back to slower CPU-bound rendering paths.

**Real case: scroll jank on a large area (GitHub issue, ~20 days old):**
- A full-page feTurbulence background made scrolling stutter. The GPU just couldn't keep up with rasterizing the SVG filter over a large area (like a full-page background).
- Promoting it to its own layer didn't fix it. The browser still struggled with the initial rasterization of the massive SVG area, and occasionally re-rasterized it during fast scrolls, causing dropped frames.
- The fix was a tiled noise.webp background image at reduced opacity, which gave silky smooth 120 FPS scrolling.
- The author also points out that SVG filters and CSS backdrop-filter are incredibly powerful, but their render cost is often hidden until you hit high-refresh-rate screens or lower-end devices.

**Mitigations:**
- Keep the filter region small. A tighter filter region reduces the pixel area recomputed on every frame.
- Avoid animating transform or position on a filtered element. Doing so forces the browser to recompute the entire filter effect every frame rather than compositing a cached layer. Pre-render the effect as a static image instead, or use will-change: filter sparingly.
- Codrops advises: keep the animations limited to smaller areas; the larger the animated area, the more resource-consuming it will be.
- For complex filter animation, driving it from JavaScript is easier to control for complex filter motion because you can throttle updates.
- For simple effects like blur, grayscale or drop-shadow, one source says CSS filter functions are much faster than SVG filters. 
- Spec background: the SVG Working Group noted that feTurbulence is not limited to the object size. For such unbounded primitives, the default filter region is -10%,-10%,120%,120%.

None of the results gave benchmark numbers for backdrop-filter specifically. It only came up in the general warning above about hidden render cost.

Here's what the two searches turned up, split into the CSS deboss part and the SVG ink-bleed part.

**Letterpress / deboss with text-shadow**
- No true inset exists: writing text-shadow: inset 2px 2px 4px black does nothing, and there is no finalised specification for inset text-shadow as of 2026.
- Basic rule: a 1px light shadow below dark text creates an embossed look. Flip it – a 1px dark shadow above light text – for an engraved effect. The illusion only works when text color and shadow color are tuned to match the background. Example: `background:#c8c4bc; color:#a8a49c; text-shadow:0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.6)`.
- Classic stamped look: choose a text colour that is darker than the background, and then create a 1px text shadow with a 1px blur and offset it down 1px. Make the text-shadow slightly lighter than the background.
- Two-shadow deboss on a dark background: `text-shadow: 1px 1px 1px rgba(255,255,255,.2), -1px -1px 1px rgba(0,0,0,.6);`. In words, a darker text shadow above and to the left, and a lighter text shadow below and to the right.
- Pitfall: high blur values on small text make the shadow bleed outside the letterforms and look more like a glow than an inset effect. Also, text-shadow doesn't render on text clipped with background-clip:text.
- A useful extra (Kinetics demo): give the paper a subtle repeating-linear-gradient texture plus `box-shadow: inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.7)`, and animate the shadow pair to fake a moving light.

**Ink bleed / rough text with SVG filters**
- Best match for the query: Carmen Ansio's article "SVG Filter Text Effects: Letterpress, Ink Gain, Woodtype". It says the same feTurbulence + feDisplacementMap stack from image distortion works directly on text. Low scale values give a subtle hand-lettered wobble. It covers ink gain, worn letterpress and woodtype, and points out there's no CSS shorthand function for feMorphology, feDisplacementMap or feConvolveMatrix, so you need `filter:url(#id)`.
- How to apply it: use the CSS property 'filter: url(#my-filter)' referencing the id of an SVG filter defined inside an svg element, typically one with width and height set to 0 and positioned absolutely so it stays invisible. The browser then renders the HTML element through that filter, including complex effects like feDisplacementMap distortion, while the text remains selectable.
- A recommended filter chain from a GitHub issue: fixed-seed feTurbulence for a stable irregular field; feDisplacementMap for bounded spatial deformation; optional light feMorphology for edge spread.
- Codrops' Heron case study (Oct 2026) builds an ink-bleed edge the same way: feTurbulence into feDisplacementMap, softened with blur and contrast.
- Typical values: MDN's example uses `baseFrequency="0.05" numOctaves="2"`. For text, keep the displacement scale small (about 1–4px). A high baseFrequency value reduces the size of the distortion pattern.

content.content:
**Title:** "Proposal: Custom Highlight API Extensions" (issue #14613 in w3c/csswg-drafts). kbabbitt opened it on **Oct 15, 2026**.

**Timeline:**
- **Oct 16:** labeled Agenda+ TPAC.
- **Oct 17–27:** placed on the TPAC 2026 agenda, then moved to the Friday Morning slot.
- **Oct 30:** the meeting bot posted the results of the CSSWG discussion.

**What the group resolved:**
1. **Opacity:** "Highlights should support opacity." It would change the opacity of the highlight background, the text and the text decoration, with "details TBD."
2. **Animations and transitions:** "Animations and transitions should be allowed on highlights." When asked, fantasai said this only means the properties would apply generally. It doesn't cover the per-character staggering idea.

**Not resolved:** Per-range styling through `getRangeStyle()` stayed open. kbabbitt said the group needed "to keep talking about per-range discussion."

**After the meeting:**
- **Oct 30:** "Needs Edits" and "Needs Testcase (WPT)" labels were added. flackr also posted comments arguing against treating opacity as a stacking context and against per-range styles.
- **Nov 3:** kbabbitt updated the explainer. Among the changes, it adds a `range-index()` option as an alternative to `getRangeStyle()`. It also adds an `auto` value for opacity, so an unset opacity can be told apart from an explicit `opacity: 1`.

The article gives the following filter recipes and performance notes.

## Ink gain / true outer stroke (`feMorphology`)
- **Why:** CSS strokes are centered on the edge, so half the stroke eats into the glyph. `dilate` grows the shape outward by exactly `radius` pixels.
- **Chain:** `feMorphology operator="dilate" radius="2" in="SourceAlpha"` → `feFlood flood-color="#884AFF"` → `feComposite operator="in"` (flood clipped to the dilated shape) → `feMerge` (stroke underneath, `SourceGraphic` on top).
- **Thinning:** `feMorphology operator="erode" radius="1"` on `SourceGraphic` makes the type look lighter. At `radius="2"`, thin faces can lose strokes.
- **Caveat:** The kernel is square, so corners square off and the stroke looks chunky at around `radius="4"`. For rounded strokes, the author suggests a duplicated `<use>` with `stroke-linejoin="round"`.

## Extreme ink gain / gooey merge
- **Chain:** `feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="7"` → `feColorMatrix` with the alpha row `0 0 0 19 -9` (a steep ramp that hardens the blurred edges) → `feComposite in="SourceGraphic" operator="atop"`.
- **Region:** `x/y="-20%"`, `width/height="140%"`.
- **Animation:** letter-spacing oscillates so neighboring letters touch and then separate.
- **Warning:** This one "fails ugly rather than gracefully," so test it before you ship it.

## Shadow woodtype (stacked `feOffset`)
- **Chain:** `feMorphology dilate radius="2"` on `SourceAlpha` → five `feOffset` steps (dx/dy 1,1 through 5,5) → `feMerge` into one extrusion → `feComposite operator="out"` against the dilated shape (keeps only the shadow) → `feFlood #E93330` + `feComposite in` → merge it under `SourceGraphic`.
- **Alternative:** A 5×5 diagonal `feConvolveMatrix` kernel also works. But you can't recolor or tween a fixed matrix, so stacked offsets are easier to animate or point in a new direction.

## Metal type under a lamp (`feSpecularLighting`)
- **Chain:** `feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="3"` on `SourceAlpha` (used as a height map) → `feSpecularLighting` (`surfaceScale="9"`, `specularConstant="1.4"`, `specularExponent="32"`, white light, `fePointLight x="220" y="-50" z="160"`) → `feComposite in` clipped to `SourceAlpha` → `feBlend mode="screen"` over the original.
- **Interaction:** JavaScript moves the point light's x/y to follow the mouse.

## Worn letterpress (`feTurbulence`)
- **Chain:** `feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.035" numOctaves="3" seed="8"` → `feDisplacementMap scale="6"`, with the x channel set to R and y to G.
- **Region:** expanded (`x="-15%" y="-30%" width="130%" height="160%"`) because displacement pushes pixels past the bounding box.
- **Scale:** Low values give a hand-lettered wobble and high values shred the letters. `fractalNoise` gives softer edges than `turbulence`.

## Gilded initial (combines the above)
- Crimson keyline: `dilate radius="3"` filled with `#5b1410` via `feFlood` + `feComposite in`.
- Gold `linearGradient` fill.
- Specular sheen: blur 1.5, `surfaceScale="3.5"`, `specularExponent="22"`, clipped to the glyph.
- Merge order: key, then source, then shine.

## Performance and practical notes
- `feTurbulence`, displacement and lighting cost the most. Several animated filters "will heat a laptop fast."
- Drive animation with `requestAnimationFrame`, and use `IntersectionObserver` so filters only recompute while on screen.
- Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` by showing a still frame instead of looping.
- Don't put filter defs in a `display: none` SVG, because Chromium drops them. Use a zero-size, absolutely positioned SVG or `visibility: hidden` instead.
- Put `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"` on every filter. The default `linearRGB` washes out blends.
- Widen the filter region for anything that bleeds outside the box.
- CSS can't animate primitive attributes, so animation has to come from JavaScript.
- `feImage` is unreliable on HTML, especially in Safari. For pattern fills, `background-clip: text` is the safer choice.

I found Figma's own blog posts about multiplayer cursors and cursor chat, plus a few third-party guides. None of the Figma posts I found say how Figma smooths remote cursor movement. Third-party tutorials point to the open-source `perfect-cursors` library for that.

**Figma's own blog posts**
- **[Multiplayer Editing in Figma](https://www.figma.com/blog/multiplayer-editing-in-figma/) (Sept 28, 2016):** This post introduces presence. It says "The first thing you'll notice when you edit something alongside someone else is their mouse cursor. We show the cursor and selection of all active participants because it provides important context." It adds that cursors can come in handy for other things too, such as waving your cursor around to get someone's attention or placing your cursor by an object to point at it.
- **[Talk it out in Figma and FigJam](https://www.figma.com/blog/talk-it-out-in-figma-and-figjam/) (Aug 31, 2021):** This post announced cursor chat. Figma launched audio and cursor chat, introducing two new ways to communicate without leaving Figma and FigJam. The goal was to recreate those magical moments—a spontaneous brainstorm at a teammate's desk or a quick chair swivel to catch-up with a co-worker. When building it, top of mind was creating a single space for users to interact with each other, so they don't have to toggle between other tools.
- **[April Fun Day cursors](https://www.figma.com/blog/april-fun-day-cursors/) (Apr 4, 2024):** This post has rendering details. In Figma and FigJam, cursors signify multiplayer collaboration. These avatars don't just design and build, but also chat, emote, and high five. Name tags needed to stretch horizontally to accommodate different name lengths. And Figma renders cursors and name tags on a per-pixel level, which means that they feel nimble and native; the downside is that they're a pain to scale.

**How cursor chat works**
- Cursor chat allows you to type live, temporary messages to other people in your Figma files, great for quick, short encounters, reactions or messages. You open it with the keyboard shortcut / and start typing; your message moves with your cursor and disappears after a few seconds ([DesignerUp](https://designerup.co/blog/5-ways-to-unlock-the-power-of-collaborate-and-communicate-in-figma/)).
- 52 characters is the hard cap per message (Figma Help Center), and viewers get cursor chat without being able to touch the design itself ([WPDean](https://wpdean.com/how-to-chat-in-figma/)).

**Smooth interpolation (third-party sources)**
- **[Vercel guide: Figma-style multiplayer cursors](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/real-time-board-nextjs-fastapi) (about 3 weeks old):** The server sends cursor snapshots as discrete points. The client uses perfect-cursors to animate each remote cursor between those points. It also uses normalized coordinates, so a cursor at { "x": 0.5, "y": 0.5 } appears in the center no matter how large the viewer's screen is.
- **[mskelton.dev: Building Figma Multiplayer Cursors](https://mskelton.dev/blog/building-figma-multiplayer-cursors):** A walkthrough that splits the work into a component that shows other users' cursors and a component that sends your own position.
- **[JavaScript in Plain English: OT vs CRDT for cursors](https://javascript.plainenglish.io/how-real-time-multiplayer-cursors-work-in-figma-and-google-docs-ot-vs-crdt-fba591f3665c):** It explains why polling falls short: the result is choppy, stuttering cursors.

If you need more on smoothing, try searching for "perfect-cursors" by Steve Ruiz (it uses spline interpolation between updates) or Liveblocks' posts on smooth cursors. That's from memory; this search didn't return those sources.

**Earlier context (separate topics):** VS Code's `editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation` takes the values off, explicit and on ([GitHub #169332](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332), [VS Code 1.30 notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_30), [Dan Schroeder's blog](https://blog.danskingdom.com/Visual-Studio-Code-default-settings-to-change/)). Monkeytype's smooth caret has a "fast" setting timed at about 85 ms ([typeTrainer PR #88](https://github.com/69inoi69/typeTrainer/pull/88), [Monkeytype discussion #1248](https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248)).

I found good material on halftone dots and riso-style grain, but no single tutorial that covers halftone, misregistration and grain together.

**Most relevant results**

- **[Codrops: Creating a Risograph Grain Light Effect in Three.js](https://tympanus.net/codrops/2022/03/07/creating-a-risograph-grain-light-effect-in-three-js/)** (2022): the closest match for riso grain. It writes a custom ShaderMaterial and uses glsl-noise for a 2D simplex noise and glslify to import the noise function directly at the beginning of the fragment shader. The grain is screen-space: `vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy; vec3 noiseColors = vec3(snoise2(uv));`. It then mixes that grain with the lighting and strengthens it with `pow()`. It starts from MeshLambertMaterial shader and adds the grain at the end of the fragment shader.
- **[glslify/glsl-halftone](https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone)** ([npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/glsl-halftone), [index.glsl](https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone/blob/master/index.glsl)): a halftone shader in GLSL, adapted from Stefan Gustavson's work. The API is `halftone(color, uv[, frequency])`, and a higher frequency (default 30.0) leads to more tiling and smaller circles. Inside the source:
  - It makes a rough RGB-to-CMYK conversion.
  - Each channel gets its own rotated dot grid, using `mat2` rotations at about 45° for K and 15° for C/M.
  - Fractal simplex noise `n` is added to the dot threshold and to the paper/ink colours, which gives an organic, uneven ink look.
  - Dot edges are antialiased with `aastep`.
  
  Misregistration isn't built in, but you can add it easily: give each ink channel a small uv offset (a constant shift or a low-frequency noise shift) before its grid lookup.
- **[Gustavson-derived halftone_cmyk.glsl (Processing examples)](https://github.com/genekogan/Processing-Shader-Examples/blob/master/TextureShaders/data/halftone_cmyk.glsl)**: the original GLSL halftone shader demo for WebGL by Stefan Gustavson 2012-02-16. It includes an antialiased step function, explicit bilinear lookup and textureless simplex noise from ashima/webgl-noise. A simpler [single-channel halftone.glsl](https://github.com/genekogan/Processing-Shader-Examples/blob/master/TextureShaders/data/halftone.glsl) is in the same repo. It pixelates into cells, then uses `step(dist, bright*pixelSize*0.8)`.
- **[Agate Dragon: Creating a halftone shader](https://agatedragon.blog/2024/03/31/halftone-shader/)** (2024): a step-by-step beginner tutorial. It covers multiplication, aspect ratio correction, conversion to greyscale, smoothing and the distance to the centre of a circle, using `fract(uv*total) - 0.5` cells.
- **[CodePen: WebGL Shader Halftone (cmalven)](https://codepen.io/cmalven/pen/mMrEbV)**: a Pixi filter version with uniforms for dotSize, frequency, white/black ink colours, `colorShift` (useful as a channel offset or misregistration control), mouse and `distortionAmount`.
- **[Wikipedia: Risograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risograph)**: background on the look. Due to it's analog processes, misregistration and its uneven textures are embraced by artists.

**Suggested riso recipe from these sources:**
1. Split the image into 2–3 spot-ink layers instead of full CMYK.
2. Draw each layer with a rotated halftone grid, as in glsl-halftone.
3. Give each layer its own uv offset or slight rotation for misregistration.
4. Add simplex noise to the dot thresholds for uneven ink.
5. Combine the layers multiplicatively over a paper colour.
6. Add screen-space grain as in the Codrops tutorial.

**Earlier related results on paper texture and normal maps** (from a previous search):
- [Tips4Devs: photo normal map](https://tips4devs.com/articles/create-a-photo-normal-map-for-threejs.html): uses a paper texture with MeshPhongMaterial.
- [ilovesprites: PBR textures](https://ilovesprites.com/blog/threejs-pbr-textures-normal-maps): colour-space and `normalScale` tips.
- [Medium: Advanced texture mapping](https://medium.com/@sohail_saifi/advanced-texture-mapping-in-three-js-make-your-3d-models-stand-out-18577bb3322b): blends two normal maps via `onBeforeCompile`.

The search turned up a lot about how Think Kit's ink rendering works. It found almost nothing on how the original watercolor and other brushes were designed.

**Think Kit's design and rendering (most useful source: FiftyThree's Medium post, "The Intention Behind Think Kit")**
- The goal was to bring Paper's immediacy to structured thinking by creating a single "diagram" tool that spans the continuum.
- The main problem was the continuum of input: there's no clear division between shapes, connectors, and everything else. Think Kit approaches this by first making its best attempt to understand the input, considering both what was drawn, and how the user drew it.
- Shape detection and rendering are closely linked: ink rendering is tightly integrated with the recognition and correction steps, and the degree of correction adapts both to what the user drew, and how they drew it. The Intention Engine controls Ink Engine parameters and stroke replay, sometimes several times over.
- For connectors: If a stroke starts or ends in a shape, but also lies partially outside the shape, Think Kit assumes it is an arrow or connector between shapes.
- Building it took a lot of prototyping. FiftyThree has always had a strong prototyping discipline, yet Think Kit required even more than usual due to the design and engineering complexity.
- Think Kit launched in May 2015 with three tools, Diagram, Cut, and Fill, [which] employ FiftyThree's trademark drawing recognition and rendering system called Intention Engine. The engine recognizes and corrects dozens of shapes and sketches in real time, while preserving a hand-drawn quality.

**Ink engine and brushes**
- Version 1.3.1 brought a new ink upgrade that introduces the Expressive Ink Engine built on OpenGL for faster rendering.
- The original tools: Draw, a fountain pen that mimics ink lines from thick to thin based on your movement, plus Sketch (a soft lead pencil), Outline (bold marker), Write (thin ink pen), Color (watercolor brush), and Mixer (an intuitive color mixing palette).
- Reviewers praised the watercolor results but didn't explain how the brush was made, e.g. beautiful strokes that appear to have been created by watercolor.

**What's missing:** none of the results explain the technical design of the watercolor brush or the other original brushes (blending, pigment simulation, and so on). Searching next for something like "FiftyThree watercolor brush engineering," "Paper by FiftyThree watercolor blending," or interviews with Andrew Allen, Georg Petschnigg, or Julian Walker might fill that in.

I found two relevant Smashing Magazine articles by Vitaly Friedman, and several other sources agree with them.

**Smashing Magazine, "Usability Pitfalls of Disabled Buttons, and How To Avoid Them" (2021)**
- Main problem: Disabled buttons don't explain what's wrong.
- Accessibility: As Adam Silver notes in his book "Form Design Patterns", disabled buttons usually aren't focusable, so keyboard users can't reach them. They also tend to have insufficient contrast, because they're meant to look different from regular buttons.
- Suggested alternative: If the button doesn't need to be disabled, validate on submit and guide users directly to errors with sensible error messages.
- Inclusive tip: change the cursor on a disabled button (cursor: not-allowed) to show it can't be used.

**Smashing Magazine, "Hidden vs. Disabled In UX" (2024)**
- Instead of removing unavailable options or buttons, consider disabling them and letting users "Hide all unavailable options." Explain why a feature is disabled and how to re-enable it.
- Further reading it lists: Disabled Buttons And What To Do Instead (Adam Silver), Disabled States (Maria Panagiotidi), Making Disabled Buttons Inclusive (Sandrina Pereira), and Alternative Design Patterns For Disabled Features (Katie Jacquez)

**Smart Interface Design Patterns (also by Friedman)**
- Instead of the usual tooltip, guide users to the form errors, either with a link to an error summary at the top of the page or with jump-links to the fields with errors. Or add a hint next to the disabled button explaining why it's disabled.
- When disabling works: for example, if an item turns out to be out of stock as you add it to your cart, disabling the "add to cart" button is reasonable to avoid confusion.

**Other sources**
- aria-disabled: use aria-disabled instead of disabled, because the button can still get focus and screen readers announce that it exists. Users can tab to it, and the screen reader says it's dimmed (VoiceOver) or disabled (ChromeVox).
- WCAG: disabled buttons don't have to meet AA colour contrast requirements.
- Never disabling: keep buttons enabled at all times and let users click them. Finding errors that way is easier than the mental effort of working out why a button is disabled.
- Also relevant: uxdesign.cc's "Never, ever disable buttons — Requirements for an accessible solution," and Axess Lab's "Disabled buttons suck," which another source cites.

Here are the three settings from the schema you pasted.

**smoothCaret**
- Enum: `"export const SmoothCaretSchema = z.enum(["off", "slow", "medium", "fast"]);"`
- It's listed in the caret group of `ConfigSchema` as `"smoothCaret: SmoothCaretSchema,"`

**caretStyle**
- Enum values: `"off"`, `"default"`, `"block"`, `"outline"`, `"underline"`, `"carrot"`, `"banana"`, `"monkey"`
- It appears as `"caretStyle: CaretStyleSchema,"`. The same set of values is also used for `"paceCaretStyle: CaretStyleSchema,"`

**smoothLineScroll**
- It's there, in the appearance group, as a plain on/off switch: `"smoothLineScroll: z.boolean(),"`

**How this compares with the earlier research**
- **Slow and medium are now confirmed:** my earlier search found only "fast" in a source, the 85 ms figure from [typeTrainer PR #88](https://github.com/69inoi69/typeTrainer/pull/88). This schema has all four speeds.
- **Smooth caret used to be on/off:** old copies of the site showed only those two options ([seerlite.github.io](https://seerlite.github.io/monkeytype/), [vntype.web.app](https://vntype.web.app/settings), [dev.monkeytype.com](https://dev.monkeytype.com/settings)). An old exported config also stored it as `"smoothCaret": true` ([gist](https://gist.github.com/Nitheesh-S/31dcdda0c35fc9f03514d8ab413d54cf)).
- **Caret styles changed:** those old copies listed shapes (off, |, ▮, ▯, _). The current enum uses names instead and adds the carrot, banana and monkey styles.
- **Speed options were requested before:** a 2021 request asked for "off, normal, fast" ([Discussion #1248](https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248)). The "fast, normal, smooth" options in the [Notesnook issue](https://github.com/streetwriters/notesnook/issues/5807) turn out to be wrong.

The halftone and risograph results ([Codrops](https://tympanus.net/codrops/2022/03/07/creating-a-risograph-grain-light-effect-in-three-js/), [glsl-halftone](https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone), [Agate Dragon](https://agatedragon.blog/2024/03/31/halftone-shader/), [CodePen](https://codepen.io/cmalven/pen/mMrEbV), [Gustavson CMYK shader](https://github.com/genekogan/Processing-Shader-Examples/blob/master/TextureShaders/data/halftone_cmyk.glsl)) have nothing to do with this question.

The article is **third-party**. Its author, Dennis Brotzky, says he has "never worked at Linear and have never seen their code." Everything comes from studying the app, Linear's blog posts and conference talks. He says the speed variables come from Linear's stylesheet, so they're likely real, but they're his observations and Linear hasn't confirmed them.

**Speed CSS variables (as quoted from Linear's stylesheet)**
- `--speed-highlightFadeIn: 0s`
- `--speed-highlightFadeOut: .15s`
- `--speed-quickTransition: .1s`
- `--speed-regularTransition: .25s`
- `--speed-slowTransition: .35s`

**Durations in the example code**
- Row hover: `background-color` over 0.12s
- Arrow icon: `transform` over 0.15s
- For comparison, the author gives Material's standard as 200ms and iOS springs as about 350ms. He says Linear's defaults are "well below the industry norm."

**Appear vs. dismiss**
- The timing is asymmetric. Hover highlights, popovers and the agent panel show up instantly (0s). When dismissed, they fade out over 150ms, which the author compares to macOS.
- Motion starts from where the element came from. The status popover "scales out of the status pill," and the agent panel slides in from its toggle.
- List items have no transitions, to keep things snappy.
- The one place the author thinks Linear is too slow is the command palette.

**Which properties animate**
- Mostly the GPU-composited ones: `transform` and `opacity`.
- Sometimes paint-only ones: `background-color` and `border-color`.
- Never layout ones: `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`.
- The inline loading screen has a `logoBackgroundPulse` keyframe: opacity goes 0 → 1 (at 70%) → 0, and scale goes 0.8 → 1.0. No duration is given.

**One inconsistency:** the conclusion says durations "sit below the 100ms cause-and-effect threshold." That doesn't match the variables the article lists, since 0.12s, 0.15s, 0.25s and 0.35s are all over 100ms.

The results show the typing animation first appeared in Office 2013 and that it was disliked from the start.

**Where it came from:**
- [Tweaks.com](https://tweaks.com/windows/65719/restore-classic-typing-behavior-in-office-2013/) describes it this way: Word 2013 includes a brand new typing animation that glides across the screen as you type and to a new line upon hitting Enter. Excel 2013 includes a similar feature where the cell selection graphic glides around the grid when using the arrow keys. It adds that some will love the new animations but others may find them distracting.
- [groovyPost](https://www.groovypost.com/howto/disable-office-2013-typing-animation/) says Office 2013 tried to get fancy with a new "smooth typing" animation. It says fast typists, at 80+ Words per minute, find it distracting because the animation causes the cursor to lag behind letters as they are typed. Commenters were split. One from October 8, 2012 wrote that the cursor kept up just fine… I actually really like this new animation feature.
- [LaptopMag](https://www.laptopmag.com/articles/office-2013-typing-animation-disable) says the animation is still in Office 2016. If you're a fast typist, this animation is particularly annoying because it feels like the animation is a little slower than you are. Microsoft doesn't include a menu option to disable Office's typing animation.
- On [Microsoft Q&A (2013)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/4848704/smooth-typing-feature-stopped-working), Word MVP Suzanne Barnhill wrote that many users dislike the smooth typing, which they find very distracting.
- The [Baruch College Helpdesk](https://helpdesk.commons.gc.cuny.edu/just-how-to-disable-the-typing-animation-feature-in-office-2013/) adds that it can likewise be turbulent if you have a slower computer system, and that turning it off turns it off for all Office programs.

**How to turn it off:** Go to HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\15.0\Common and create a new key called Graphics. Then, create a new dword called DisableAnimations and set its value to 1. For Office 2016 and later, use 16.0 instead of 15.0. Note that [VersedTech](http://versedtech.org/11561/disable-typing-animation-office-2013/) names the value "DisableAnimation", without the "s". That looks like a typo, since the other sources all use "DisableAnimations".

# iA Writer Focus Mode (Mac)

**What it's for:** The page says Focus Mode "emphasizes the active sentence or paragraph while eliminating distractions," so you can concentrate on what you're working on right now.

**How to turn it on:** Use the Focus menu (Focus → Enable Focus Mode), press ⌘D, or click the button in the title bar. Then pick one of three settings:

- **Sentence:** "The active sentence is highlighted while the surrounding text is dimmed."
- **Paragraph:** The whole paragraph you're in is highlighted and everything else is dimmed. When you move the cursor into another paragraph, that one becomes the highlighted one.
- **Typewriter:** Nothing is highlighted or dimmed. Instead, the cursor stays centered vertically on screen while you type or move up and down, much like a mechanical typewriter. On iA's page, Typewriter is one of the three Focus Mode settings, not a separate feature.

**On "fading":** The page only says that surrounding text is "dimmed." It doesn't say how dim it gets, whether the change is animated, or how long any transition takes.

**Reasons and tips the page gives:**
- Users say it works best in full-screen dark mode. iA suggests trying both dark text on white and light text on dark to see which suits you.
- Use it while drafting and turn it off when editing. Selecting text to edit can clash with the cursor-centering, which can make the screen jump up and down.

I found the source and a few newer pieces that tie it to Gmail's Undo Send.

**The original article:** Aza Raskin's essay is called "Never Use a Warning When You Mean Undo." A List Apart published it on July 13, 2007. The original URL was http://www.alistapart.com/articles/neveruseawarning. It looks at "are you sure" warnings, explains how they fail (you want to delete almost everything quickly, except for the things you delete by accident), and argues that undo is often the better fix.

**Why confirmation dialogs fail:** Raskin argues that people form habits and click through confirmation dialogs. A 2026 essay says this is not a character flaw but habituation, the subject of Raskin's 2007 essay. The idea goes back further. Jef Raskin, who led the original Macintosh project, built The Humane Interface around universal undo, arguing that if every action can be reversed, warning screens become unnecessary because people ignore them out of habit anyway.

**Gmail Undo Send as the example of delayed commit:**
- Gmail holds the message for a short delay before it goes out: 5 seconds by default, up to 30 (per Google). Undo works because the side effect is held back or can be reversed.
- Interface Lineage calls this "delayed commit over confirmation." Its point: a question before sending asks people to predict a mistake, while a visible delay lets them fix one they've noticed. Questions that repeat get familiar enough to dismiss without reading.
- Timeline: Jef Raskin's The Humane Interface (2000), Aza Raskin's essay (13 July 2007), Gmail's Labs launch (19 March 2009), and Undo Send becoming a standard setting (23 June 2015).

**When a confirmation still makes sense:** When you delete a GitHub repository, GitHub warns that it can't be undone and makes you type the repository's full name. That's deliberate friction a habituated finger can't fake, and it's the right way to use a high-friction confirmation: rare, specific, and kept for actions that are truly permanent.

**Related:** Raskin also wrote "Undo Made Easy with Ajax" on Humanized, which shows how to build it. In that version, items aren't actually deleted when the user clicks delete; the deletion happens later, in an onUnload hook.

- Summary from the issue page: "For millions of people with vertigo and inner ear problems, large-scale web animations can trigger nausea, migraines, and dizziness." Its main point is that we don't need to eliminate animation; we need to apply it more thoughtfully.
- Method: To find out which web animations trigger people with vestibular disorders, she talked with Greg Tarnoff and Craig Grannell about their experiences.
- It names specific vestibular disorders, including benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and labyrinthitis, and says people with vestibular disorders aren't the only ones who can be triggered by animation on screen.
- The article has sections titled "Identifying potentially triggering animation" and "Designing safer motion." The snippets don't show what those sections say, so the specific triggers (for example scaling, spinning, or parallax) are not confirmed by these results.

**Influence:** The article is cited in the [WCAG 2.1 GitHub issue #18 ("Animation from interactions")](https://github.com/w3c/wcag21/issues/18) as a good overview of vestibular disorders on A List Apart from a web design point of view. The NN/g source articles confirm all three limits. Their main progress-indicator rule is a percent-done indicator for anything over about 10 seconds.

**Main source:** NN/g's ["Response Times: The 3 Important Limits"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/) by Jakob Nielsen, first published January 1, 1993. Its summary says the 3 main response time limits are determined by human perceptual abilities.

- **0.1 second:** Limit for users feeling that they are directly manipulating objects in the UI.
- **1 second:** Limit for users feeling that they are freely navigating the command space without having to unduly wait for the computer. The article's example: if sorting a table according to the selected column can't be done in 0.1 seconds, it certainly has to be done in 1 second, or users will feel that the UI is sluggish and will lose the sense of "flow".
- **10 seconds:** Limit for users keeping their attention on the task. Assume that users will need to reorient themselves when they return to the UI after a delay of more than 10 seconds.

**Progress-indicator guidance (same article):**
- As a rule of thumb, percent-done progress indicators should be used for operations taking more than about 10 seconds.
- Anything slower than 10 seconds needs a percent-done indicator as well as a clearly signposted way for the user to interrupt the operation.
- Feedback during the delay is especially important if the response time is likely to be highly variable, since users will then not know what to expect.
- Delays of longer than 10 seconds are only acceptable during natural breaks in the user's work, for example when switching tasks.

**Related NN/g pages:**
- [NN/g's response-time topic page](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/response-time/) lists a September 2020 video, "Mask Interaction Delays with Progress Indicators." Its advice: in case of slow response times in a user interface, indicate that the wait time will soon be over by showing an animation. For longer delays use a percent-done indicator.
- ["Powers of 10: Time Scales in User Experience"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/powers-of-10-time-scales-in-ux/) (2009) adds: if it takes longer than 0.1 seconds for the revised state to appear, then the response doesn't feel instantaneous — instead, it feels as if the computer is doing something to make the menu open. It also says that with 1-second responses users retain the feeling of being in control of the interaction even though they notice that it's a 2-way interaction.
- **Origins:** Nielsen's 1993 limits drew on Miller's 1968 work on response time in man-computer conversational transactions and Card and colleagues in 1991 ([Boostbery](https://boostbery.com/insights/why-your-brain-hates-slow-websites-the-psychology-of-page-speed/)).

# Animation rules from Emil Kowalski's STANDARDS.md

## Frequency-based rules
- **Used 100+ times a day** (keyboard shortcuts, command palette): no animation at all.
- **Used tens of times a day** (hover effects, list navigation): remove the animation or cut it back a lot.
- **Occasional** (modals, drawers, toasts): use a standard animation.
- **Rare or first-time** (onboarding, celebrations): delight is fine here.
- **Keyboard-initiated actions:** never animate them. Raycast is the example, since it has no open/close animation.
- **Valid reasons for motion:** spatial consistency, showing state, explanation, feedback, or avoiding a jarring change. "It looks cool" on a frequently seen element doesn't count.

## Durations
| Element | Duration |
|---|---|
| Button press feedback | 100–160ms |
| Tooltips, small popovers | 125–200ms |
| Dropdowns, selects | 150–250ms |
| Modals, drawers | 200–500ms |
| Marketing / explanatory | Can be longer |

- **General limit:** "UI animations stay under 300ms."
- **Stagger:** 30–80ms between items. Never block interaction while it plays.

## Easing
- **Entering or exiting:** `ease-out` (also the default).
- **Moving or morphing on screen:** `ease-in-out`.
- **Hover or color changes:** `ease`.
- **Constant motion:** `linear`.
- **`ease-in`:** never use it on UI, because it delays the moment the user is watching.
- **Custom curves** (the built-in CSS ones are too weak):
  - Strong ease-out: `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`
  - Strong ease-in-out: `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`
  - iOS-like drawer: `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`
- **Springs:** keep bounce between 0.1 and 0.3. The suggested config is `{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }`.

## Properties to animate
- **Only `transform` and `opacity`.** Animating padding, margin, height, width, top or left triggers layout and paint as well.
- **Child transforms:** set `transform` on the element itself rather than through a CSS variable on the parent.
- **Blur for crossfades:** keep it under 20px.

## Scale-from values
- **Starting scale:** never `scale(0)`. Start from 0.9–0.97 with `opacity: 0`.
- **Press feedback:** `scale(0.97)` on `:active` with a 160ms ease-out transition. The subtle range is 0.95–0.98.

## Origin-aware
- **Popovers:** scale from the trigger using `transform-origin: var(--transform-origin)`.
- **Modals:** these are the exception and stay at `transform-origin: center`.

## Interruptibility
- **Transitions vs. keyframes:** CSS transitions can be retargeted mid-animation, but keyframes restart from zero. Use transitions for anything triggered rapidly, like toasts and toggles.
- **Springs:** they keep their velocity when interrupted, which makes them good for gestures the user might reverse.
- **Entry without JS:** use `@starting-style`.

## Reduced motion
- **Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`:** keep opacity and color changes, and drop motion based on transform or position.
- **Not all-or-nothing:** reduced motion means "fewer and gentler animations, not zero."
- **Hover motion:** gate it behind `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, since touch devices fire false hovers.
- **In JS:** use `useReducedMotion()`, for example setting the closed offset to 0.

---
**Related, from your extra context:** Nielsen's [response time limits](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/) are 0.1 seconds for feeling direct, 1 second for keeping flow and 10 seconds for keeping attention. They line up with the timing rules above. See also [Powers of 10](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/powers-of-10-time-scales-in-ux/) and the [NN/g response-time topic page](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/response-time/).

- Honor prefers-reduced-motion. Provide a reduced-motion variant.
- Implementation preference. Prefer CSS, avoid main-thread JS-driven animations when possible. Preference: CSS > Web Animations API > JavaScript libraries e.g., motion.

- Easing fits the subject. Choose easing based on what changes (size, distance, trigger).
- Interruptible. Animations are cancelable by user input.
- Input-driven. Avoid autoplay except for muted, non-essential loops. Automatically playing motion lasting >5 seconds alongside other content has pause, stop, or hide controls.

The search turned up many implementations of hold-to-confirm with a progress ring and some advice on keyboard alternatives. Nothing came back about Apple Watch, Tesla or Revolut specifically. The only real-product precedents named are capture rings in other apps.

**Real-product precedents**
- One velvet-ui pull request cites press-and-hold capture rings (Instagram/Snapchat story capture, Apple Camera QuickTake) — the "charge a ring while held" affordance. These are camera capture controls, not delete actions.

**Keyboard approaches**
1. **Hold Space/Enter (most common).** DinachiUI: Space and Enter hold, and key up releases. Auto-repeat is ignored, so a held key is one hold rather than a restart on every repeat. It also cancels on blur, because a hold that continues once the button is unfocused is one the user can no longer watch. CodeFronts does the same: keyboard users hold Space/Enter via keydown/keyup — the same path. The button's aria-label says "Hold to close" up front.
2. **Tap fallback / confirm dialog.** Lepid-design issue #29 (Sept 2026) says a held Space/Enter is a poor gesture. Keyboard users get an alternative: keydown starts the same timer, keyup cancels, mirroring pointer — and the component exposes an escape hatch (confirmOnKeyboardTap) so callers can opt into a plain activate-to-fire for keyboard, falling back to a ConfirmDialog.
3. **Screen readers confirm with a single activation.** Beste UI: screen readers, which cannot hold, confirm with a single activation unless that is turned off. In SwiftUI, velvet-ui does this with .accessibilityAction lets VoiceOver confirm with a single activation (no timed hold required).

**Design details**
- **Timing varies:** about 300 ms in Lepid, 800 ms in Kinetics, 900 ms in CodeFronts, 1600 ms by default in DinachiUI and 2 s in Dzialowski's version. DinachiUI uses asymmetric timing: progress takes duration to complete but unwinds in 200ms.
- **Accessible name:** Give a ring button an aria-label. It has an outline and an icon, and neither is a name.
- **Release early:** in velvet-ui the ring springs back, no confirm, .light haptic, and under Reduce Motion the ring still shows progress.
- **General advice:** Keep a visible focus state for controls, offer a button alternative to gestures, and respect reduced-motion preferences.

**Criticisms**
- It could become frustrating if, for instance, you're attempting to delete numerous items and are required to wait for a 2-second delay with each deletion. Also, users might not immediately grasp that holding the button is necessary instead of just clicking it.
- OlegWock says it probably won't replace GitHub-like confirmation (at least if you care about accessibility).

**What's missing:** there's no documentation of how Apple Watch, Tesla or Revolut handle hold-to-confirm, and none of these sources ties the pattern to specific WCAG criteria. A narrower search per product, such as "Revolut hold to confirm" or "watchOS long press destructive," could fill that gap.

<!--

# Motion

Beautiful, fluid motions bring the interface to life, conveying status, providing feedback and instruction, and enriching the visual experience of your app or game.

## Discussion

![A sketch of three overlapping diamonds, suggesting the movement of an element from left to right. The image is overlaid with rectangular and circular grid lines and is tinted yellow to subtly reflect the yellow in the original six-color Apple logo.](images/com.apple.HIG/foundations-motion-intro@2x.png)

Many system components automatically include motion, letting you offer familiar and consistent experiences throughout your app or game. System components might also adjust their motion in response to factors like accessibility settings or different input methods. For example, the movement of [Liquid Glass](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/materials#Liquid-Glass) responds to direct touch interaction with greater emphasis to reinforce the feeling of a tactile experience, but produces a more subdued effect when a person interacts using a trackpad.

If you design custom motion, follow the guidelines below.

## Best practices

**Add motion purposefully, supporting the experience without overshadowing it.** Don’t add motion for the sake of adding motion. Gratuitous or excessive animation can distract people and may make them feel disconnected or physically uncomfortable.

**Make motion optional.** Not everyone can or wants to experience the motion in your app or game, so it’s essential to avoid using it as the only way to communicate important information. To help everyone enjoy your app or game, supplement visual feedback by also using alternatives like [haptics](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics) and [audio](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio) to communicate.

## Providing feedback

**Strive for realistic feedback motion that follows people’s gestures and expectations.** In nongame apps, accurate, realistic motion can help people understand how something works, but feedback motion that doesn’t make sense can make them feel disoriented. For example, if someone reveals a view by sliding it down from the top, they don’t expect to dismiss the view by sliding it to the side.

**Aim for brevity and precision in feedback animations.** When animated feedback is brief and precise, it tends to feel lightweight and unobtrusive, and it can often convey information more effectively than prominent animation. For example, when a game displays a succinct animation that’s precisely tied to a successful action, players can instantly get the message without being distracted from their gameplay. Another example is in visionOS: When people tap a panorama in Photos, it quickly and smoothly expands to fill the space in front of them, helping them track the transition without making them wait to enjoy the content.

**In apps, generally avoid adding motion to UI interactions that occur frequently.** The system already provides subtle animations for interactions with standard interface elements. For a custom element, you generally want to avoid making people spend extra time paying attention to unnecessary motion every time they interact with it.

**Let people cancel motion.** As much as possible, don’t make people wait for an animation to complete before they can do anything, especially if they have to experience the animation more than once.

**Consider using animated symbols where it makes sense.** When you use SF Symbols 5 or later, you can apply animations to SF Symbols or custom symbols. For guidance, see [Animations](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/sf-symbols#Animations).

## Leveraging platform capabilities

**Make sure your game’s motion looks great by default on each platform you support.** In most games, maintaining a consistent frame rate of 30 to 60 fps typically results in a smooth, visually appealing experience. For each platform you support, use the device’s graphics capabilities to enable default settings that let people enjoy your game without first having to change those settings.

**Let people customize the visual experience of your game to optimize performance or battery life.** For example, consider letting people switch between power modes when the system detects the presence of an external power source.

## Platform considerations

*No additional considerations for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or tvOS.*

### visionOS

In addition to subtly communicating context, drawing attention to information, and enriching immersive experiences, motion in visionOS can combine with [depth](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/spatial-layout#Depth) to provide essential feedback when people look at interactive elements. Because motion is likely to be a large part of your visionOS experience, it’s crucial to avoid causing distraction, confusion, or discomfort.

**As much as possible, avoid displaying motion at the edges of a person’s field of view.** People can be particularly sensitive to motion that occurs in their peripheral vision: in addition to being distracting, such motion can even cause discomfort because it can make people feel like they or their surroundings are moving. If you need to show an object moving in the periphery during an immersive experience, make sure the object’s brightness level is similar to the rest of the visible content.

**Help people remain comfortable when showing the movement of large virtual objects.** If an object is large enough to fill a lot of the [field of view](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/spatial-layout#Field-of-view), occluding most or all of [passthrough](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/immersive-experiences#Immersion-and-passthrough), people can naturally perceive it as being part of their surroundings. To help people perceive the object’s movement without making them think that they or their surroundings are moving, you can increase the object’s translucency, helping people see through it, or lower its contrast to make its motion less noticeable.

> Note: People can experience discomfort even when they’re the ones moving a large virtual object, such as a window. Although adjusting translucency and contrast can help in this scenario, consider also keeping a window’s size fairly small.

**Consider using fades when you need to relocate an object.** When an object moves from one location to another, people naturally watch the movement. If such movement doesn’t communicate anything useful to people, you can fade the object out before moving it and fade it back in after it’s in the new location.

**In general, avoid letting people rotate a virtual world.** When a virtual world rotates, the experience typically upsets people’s sense of stability, even when they control the rotation and the movement is subtle. Instead, consider using instantaneous directional changes during a quick fade-out.

**Consider giving people a stationary frame of reference.** It can be easier for people to handle visual movement when it’s contained within an area that doesn’t move. In contrast, if the entire surrounding area appears to move — for example, in a game that automatically moves a player through space — people can feel unwell.

**Avoid showing objects that oscillate in a sustained way.** In particular, you want to avoid showing an oscillation that has a frequency of around 0.2 Hz because people can be very sensitive to this frequency. If you need to show objects oscillating, aim to keep the amplitude low and consider making the content translucent.

### watchOS

SwiftUI provides a powerful and streamlined way to add motion to your app. If you need to use WatchKit to animate layout and appearance changes — or create animated image sequences — see <doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/WatchKit/WKInterfaceImage>.

> Note: All layout- and appearance-based animations automatically include built-in easing that plays at the start and end of the animation. You can’t turn off or customize easing.

Links: [{"title":"Our Guide to the Teenage Engineering OP-1","url":"https://www.soundtech.co.uk/musicians-blog/our-guide-to-the-teenage-engineering-op-1.html"},{"title":"OP-1 overview - teenage engineering","url":"https://teenage.engineering/products/op-1/original/overview"},{"title":"teenage engineering: op 1 portable synthesizer","url":"https://www.designboom.com/technology/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable-synthesizer/"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering OP-1","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering_OP-1"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering OP-1 — Motion Design","url":"https://abduzeedo.com/teenage-engineering-op1-motion-design-"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering's OP-1 Instrument: Hands-on, Videos, Why it's Different - CDM Create Digital Music","url":"https://cdm.link/teenage-engineerings-op-1-instrument-hands-on-videos-why-its-different/"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering: Constraints as Aesthetic","url":"https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering"},{"title":"Teenage Engineering OP-1: The portable synth that turned music-making into a four-track instrument","url":"https://thesynthsource.com/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable/"}]

Teenage Engineering's own page, design press and recent design essays all say the same thing about the OP-1: its animated screen graphics and color coding are the core of the interface.

**What Teenage Engineering says ([official overview](https://teenage.engineering/products/op-1/original/overview)):**
- The vector-based graphical user interface is displayed on the brilliant super AMOLED display running at 60 fps.
- All graphics run in realtime, so when a modulator is assigned to a synthesizer parameter, you'll see how that specific parameter is animated, telling you exactly what's going on.
- The four colored encoders and the symbols on the keyboard are designed for easy reading and to make controlling and shaping sounds intuitive and non-technical.
- Screen specs: a 320 × 160 colour AMOLED display with a vector-based graphical interface ([The Synth Source](https://thesynthsource.com/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable/)).

**Analysis and commentary:**
- **[Soundtech](https://www.soundtech.co.uk/musicians-blog/our-guide-to-the-teenage-engineering-op-1.html):** The screen offers a window into Teenage Engineering's clever and playful user interface design. Wordy parameters and complex menu systems are replaced with imaginative scenes and interactive imagery.
- **[CDM (Create Digital Music), 2011 hands-on](https://cdm.link/teenage-engineerings-op-1-instrument-hands-on-videos-why-its-different/):** The writer calls the OP-1's biggest achievement making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. The article's video shows how physical interactions map to iconic, graphic feedback.
- **[Blake Crosley, "Constraints as Aesthetic"](https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering):** He argues that the OP-1's single screen and four knobs forced interface designs that professionals find faster than full-featured DAWs. He says Teenage Engineering's interfaces have depth, texture, and character; they simply refuse to pretend a synth screen is an analog control panel, and that waveforms dance, tape reels spin, the mixer shows bouncing levels.
- **[The Synth Source](https://thesynthsource.com/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable/) (about 18 days old):** The colour-coded encoders and animated display reduce the distance between a parameter and its consequence. It also gives the downside: a user accustomed to conventional synthesizers may find the colour system, mode structure, and tape-centric workflow initially opaque. It says the OP-1's display, colour assignments, four main modes, graphical animation, and tape metaphor made the interface inseparable from the instrument's identity.
- **[designboom](https://www.designboom.com/technology/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable-synthesizer/):** The colour-coded interface matches coloured buttons to the graphics on the OLED display. The article includes screenshots of the synth engine, drum sampler, tape, EQ, mixer and LFO screens.
- **Awards ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering_OP-1)):** The OP-1 won one of Sweden's Design S Awards in 2012. The jury called it "A technological product which through a clever colour scheme and fantastic graphics is intuitive, easily accessible and incredibly inviting."
- **Not about the screen UI:** [Abduzeedo's "OP-1 Motion Design"](https://abduzeedo.com/teenage-engineering-op1-motion-design-) covers CGI promo animations made by Bark & Bite, not the on-device interface.

**Sources from earlier, unrelated searches (not related to the OP-1):**
- Figma multiplayer cursors: [Multiplayer Editing in Figma](https://www.figma.com/blog/multiplayer-editing-in-figma/), [Talk it out in Figma and FigJam](https://www.figma.com/blog/talk-it-out-in-figma-and-figjam/), [April Fun Day cursors](https://www.figma.com/blog/april-fun-day-cursors/), [Vercel guide](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/real-time-board-nextjs-fastapi), [mskelton.dev](https://mskelton.dev/blog/building-figma-multiplayer-cursors), [DesignerUp](https://designerup.co/blog/5-ways-to-unlock-the-power-of-collaborate-and-communicate-in-figma/), [WPDean](https://wpdean.com/how-to-chat-in-figma/), [JavaScript in Plain English](https://javascript.plainenglish.io/how-real-time-multiplayer-cursors-work-in-figma-and-google-docs-ot-vs-crdt-fba591f3665c)
- VS Code and Monkeytype smooth caret: [VS Code #169332](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332), [VS Code 1.30 notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_30), [Dan Schroeder](https://blog.danskingdom.com/Visual-Studio-Code-default-settings-to-change/), [typeTrainer PR #88](https://github.com/69inoi69/typeTrainer/pull/88), [Monkeytype #1248](https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248)
- Vercel animation guidelines: [Web Interface Guidelines](https://vercel.com/design/guidelines), [command.md](https://github.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/blob/main/command.md) ([raw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md)), [web-animation-design skill](https://mcpservers.org/agent-skills/vercel/web-animation-design), [open-agents SKILL.md](https://github.com/vercel-labs/open-agents/blob/main/.agents/skills/web-animation-design/SKILL.md), [UIChemy](https://uichemy.com/design-skills/web-design-guidelines/)
- Apple HIG on motion: [current page](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md), [older Foundations page](https://developers.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/foundations/motion), [Use Your Loaf](https://useyourloaf.com/blog/reducing-motion-of-animations/), [Uxcel](https://uxcel.com/lessons/accessibility-inclusion-standards-812)
- Rauno Freiberg's "Invisible Details of Interaction Design": [X post](https://x.com/raunofreiberg/status/1678438662399221761), [Learn UI](https://learn-ui.com/chapters/invisible-details)
- Shimmer "thinking" text: [WireKit](https://docs.wirekit.app/components/shimmer), [GPUI Kit](https://gpui-kit.com/component/shimmer/), [explainx.ai](https://explainx.ai/blog/ai-aesthetic-design-patterns-jim-nielsen-2026)

Web search results for query: "AI chat "thinking" shimmer text indicator criticism "fake progress" OR "theatre" reasoning trace UX 2025"

Links: [{"title":"Reasoning Theater: Your AI Is Faking It - Uday","url":"https://udaykamath.substack.com/p/reasoning-theater-your-ai-is-faking"},{"title":"Reasoning Theater: When AI Pretends to Think","url":"https://www.emergentmind.com/videos/reasoning-theater-disentangling-cot-beliefs-b8cf6292"},{"title":"Design Theater: Evaluating the Gap Between User-Facing Design Reasoning and Implementation in Generative UI Tools","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.22928"},{"title":"80% of Your AI's Thinking May Be Theatre","url":"https://marekkowal.substack.com/p/the-spin-cycle"},{"title":"Design Theater: A Benchmark for Generative UI","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2607.22928v1"},{"title":"When Reasoning Models “Show Their Work,” Can You Actually Trust It?","url":"https://medium.com/@Micheal-Lanham/when-reasoning-models-show-their-work-can-you-actually-trust-it-58f8c377e253"},{"title":"Reasoning Theater: Why Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Fails Your Agentic AI","url":"https://www.rockcybermusings.com/p/reasoning-theater-cot-monitoring-fails-agentic-ai"},{"title":"ReTrace: Interactive Visualizations for Reasoning Traces of Large Reasoning Models","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.11187"},{"title":"Illusion of thinking: Apple's study highlights advanced AI flaws confusing verbosity with cognition","url":"https://www.milwaukeeindependent.com/explainers/illusion-thinking-apples-study-highlights-advanced-ai-flaws-confusing-verbosity-cognition/"}]

I found almost nothing that criticizes the shimmer "thinking" indicator itself as fake progress. What I did find is a lot of 2026 criticism of the reasoning trace as "theater," plus one paper that applies the idea to generative UI tools.

**"Reasoning Theater" (Goodfire AI and Harvard, arXiv:2603.05488)**
- The paper's claim is that models internally commit to answers early but continue generating reasoning text as if uncertainty remains.
- Its key number: at the 5% mark of the reasoning trace, barely a few sentences into the model's "thinking," the model can already produce its correct final answer with 65% accuracy on recall-based questions.
- The finding has limits. On hard questions requiring genuine multistep reasoning, CoT remains a valuable signal.
- The sources disagree on the date. One says a March 2025 paper, but the arXiv ID and [Lanham's Medium piece](https://medium.com/@Micheal-Lanham/when-reasoning-models-show-their-work-can-you-actually-trust-it-58f8c377e253) point to a March 2026 paper. 2026 is the likely date.

**Commentary that touches the UX side**
- [Marek Kowal's "80% of Your AI's Thinking May Be Theatre"](https://marekkowal.substack.com/p/the-spin-cycle) comes closest to criticizing the UI. He writes, "I think many of us are doing the same thing with AI reasoning. We watch the 'thinking' animation pulse." He also cites the Basu & Chakraborty paper, "When AI Shows Its Work, Is It Actually Working?" (arXiv:2603.22816).
- [Lanham on Medium](https://medium.com/@Micheal-Lanham/when-reasoning-models-show-their-work-can-you-actually-trust-it-58f8c377e253) puts it this way: "You're paying for tokens that look like thinking but function more like narration."
- Other write-ups of the same research: [Uday Kamath's Substack](https://udaykamath.substack.com/p/reasoning-theater-your-ai-is-faking), [Emergent Mind](https://www.emergentmind.com/videos/reasoning-theater-disentangling-cot-beliefs-b8cf6292) and [RockCyber Musings](https://www.rockcybermusings.com/p/reasoning-theater-cot-monitoring-fails-agentic-ai).

**HCI research on reasoning traces**
- ["Design Theater" (arXiv:2607.22928)](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.22928v1) checks whether generative UI tools actually build what their reasoning says. It notes that users treat reasoning traces as trust-calibration tools, and that the presentation of rationales alone can shape trust in AI decisions, even when the underlying model behavior remains unchanged.
- [ReTrace (arXiv:2511.11187)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.11187) is a more positive take: interactive visualizations of the trace helped participants to see strategies, points of confidence, and uncertainty.
- There's also a [Milwaukee Independent explainer on Apple's "Illusion of Thinking" study](https://www.milwaukeeindependent.com/explainers/illusion-thinking-apples-study-highlights-advanced-ai-flaws-confusing-verbosity-cognition/).

**From the earlier searches you passed along**
- On shimmer as a design pattern: [explainx.ai on Jim Nielsen's "AI aesthetic"](https://explainx.ai/blog/ai-aesthetic-design-patterns-jim-nielsen-2026), plus component docs from [GPUI Kit](https://gpui-kit.com/component/shimmer/) (which says shimmer shows activity, not progress), [TurboStarter](https://www.turbostarter.dev/ai/docs/components/shimmer), [WireKit](https://docs.wirekit.app/components/shimmer), [Create UI](https://createui.co/docs/components/text-shimmer), [ElevenLabs UI](https://ui.elevenlabs.io/docs/components/shimmering-text), [21st.dev](https://21st.dev/@ElevenLabs/components/shimmering-text), [PanelUI](https://panelui.dev/docs/ai-components/shimmer) and [Patterns.dev](https://www.patterns.dev/react/ai-ui-patterns/).
- On response times: [NN/g Response Time Limits](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/), [NN/g Powers of 10](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/powers-of-10-time-scales-in-ux/), [NN/g response-time topic page](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/response-time/), [UX Collective, "The waiting problem in AI products"](https://uxdesign.cc/the-waiting-problem-in-ai-products-e7c11fd5a825?gi=226235e5daa0), [Boostbery](https://boostbery.com/insights/why-your-brain-hates-slow-websites-the-psychology-of-page-speed/), [Hello Retail](https://helloretail.com/en/blog/2026-10-09-fast-site-search-ecommerce/), [WebYes](https://www.webyes.com/blogs/good-website-response-time/), [Global Bridge Labs](https://globalbridgelabs.co.uk/blogs/how-long-visitors-wait-for-website) and a [Facebook answers page](https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/nielsen-norman-response-times-0-1-1-10-seconds-user-experience/).
- On interaction craft (no shimmer content): Rauno Freiberg's "Invisible Details of Interaction Design," via [X](https://x.com/raunofreiberg/status/1678438662399221761), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/REDACTED), [Learn UI](https://learn-ui.com/chapters/invisible-details), [Fountn](https://fountn.design/resource/invisible-details-of-interaction-design/), [UI/UX Showcase](https://uiuxshowcase.com/resources/invisible-details-of-interaction-design-by-rauno-freiberg/) and [yespress](https://yespress.io/rauno-freiberg).
- Unrelated to this topic: [Apple HIG Motion](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md), the [older HIG Motion page](https://developers.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/foundations/motion), [Use Your Loaf](https://useyourloaf.com/blog/reducing-motion-of-animations/), [Uxcel](https://uxcel.com/lessons/accessibility-inclusion-standards-812), [Wikipedia: WebGPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebGPU), [web.dev](https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers), [Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/webgpu/overview) and [Cinevva](https://app.cinevva.com/guides/webgl-webgpu-not-supported-fix).

**Gap:** No result directly calls the shimmer or "Thinking…" label fake progress. The UX Collective "waiting problem" article and Jim Nielsen's original post look like the best next searches.
