# Motion

Beautiful, fluid motions bring the interface to life, conveying status, providing feedback and instruction, and enriching the visual experience of your app or game.

## Discussion

![A sketch of three overlapping diamonds, suggesting the movement of an element from left to right. The image is overlaid with rectangular and circular grid lines and is tinted yellow to subtly reflect the yellow in the original six-color Apple logo.](images/com.apple.HIG/foundations-motion-intro@2x.png)

Many system components automatically include motion, letting you offer familiar and consistent experiences throughout your app or game. System components might also adjust their motion in response to factors like accessibility settings or different input methods. For example, the movement of [Liquid Glass](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/materials#Liquid-Glass) responds to direct touch interaction with greater emphasis to reinforce the feeling of a tactile experience, but produces a more subdued effect when a person interacts using a trackpad.

If you design custom motion, follow the guidelines below.

## Best practices

**Add motion purposefully, supporting the experience without overshadowing it.** Don’t add motion for the sake of adding motion. Gratuitous or excessive animation can distract people and may make them feel disconnected or physically uncomfortable.

**Make motion optional.** Not everyone can or wants to experience the motion in your app or game, so it’s essential to avoid using it as the only way to communicate important information. To help everyone enjoy your app or game, supplement visual feedback by also using alternatives like [haptics](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics) and [audio](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio) to communicate.

## Providing feedback

**Strive for realistic feedback motion that follows people’s gestures and expectations.** In nongame apps, accurate, realistic motion can help people understand how something works, but feedback motion that doesn’t make sense can make them feel disoriented. For example, if someone reveals a view by sliding it down from the top, they don’t expect to dismiss the view by sliding it to the side.

**Aim for brevity and precision in feedback animations.** When animated feedback is brief and precise, it tends to feel lightweight and unobtrusive, and it can often convey information more effectively than prominent animation. For example, when a game displays a succinct animation that’s precisely tied to a successful action, players can instantly get the message without being distracted from their gameplay. Another example is in visionOS: When people tap a panorama in Photos, it quickly and smoothly expands to fill the space in front of them, helping them track the transition without making them wait to enjoy the content.

**In apps, generally avoid adding motion to UI interactions that occur frequently.** The system already provides subtle animations for interactions with standard interface elements. For a custom element, you generally want to avoid making people spend extra time paying attention to unnecessary motion every time they interact with it.

**Let people cancel motion.** As much as possible, don’t make people wait for an animation to complete before they can do anything, especially if they have to experience the animation more than once.

**Consider using animated symbols where it makes sense.** When you use SF Symbols 5 or later, you can apply animations to SF Symbols or custom symbols. For guidance, see [Animations](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/sf-symbols#Animations).

## Leveraging platform capabilities

**Make sure your game’s motion looks great by default on each platform you support.** In most games, maintaining a consistent frame rate of 30 to 60 fps typically results in a smooth, visually appealing experience. For each platform you support, use the device’s graphics capabilities to enable default settings that let people enjoy your game without first having to change those settings.

**Let people customize the visual experience of your game to optimize performance or battery life.** For example, consider letting people switch between power modes when the system detects the presence of an external power source.

## Platform considerations

*No additional considerations for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or tvOS.*

### visionOS

In addition to subtly communicating context, drawing attention to information, and enriching immersive experiences, motion in visionOS can combine with [depth](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/spatial-layout#Depth) to provide essential feedback when people look at interactive elements. Because motion is likely to be a large part of your visionOS experience, it’s crucial to avoid causing distraction, confusion, or discomfort.

**As much as possible, avoid displaying motion at the edges of a person’s field of view.** People can be particularly sensitive to motion that occurs in their peripheral vision: in addition to being distracting, such motion can even cause discomfort because it can make people feel like they or their surroundings are moving. If you need to show an object moving in the periphery during an immersive experience, make sure the object’s brightness level is similar to the rest of the visible content.

**Help people remain comfortable when showing the movement of large virtual objects.** If an object is large enough to fill a lot of the [field of view](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/spatial-layout#Field-of-view), occluding most or all of [passthrough](/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/immersive-experiences#Immersion-and-passthrough), people can naturally perceive it as being part of their surroundings. To help people perceive the object’s movement without making them think that they or their surroundings are moving, you can increase the object’s translucency, helping people see through it, or lower its contrast to make its motion less noticeable.

> Note: People can experience discomfort even when they’re the ones moving a large virtual object, such as a window. Although adjusting translucency and contrast can help in this scenario, consider also keeping a window’s size fairly small.

**Consider using fades when you need to relocate an object.** When an object moves from one location to another, people naturally watch the movement. If such movement doesn’t communicate anything useful to people, you can fade the object out before moving it and fade it back in after it’s in the new location.

**In general, avoid letting people rotate a virtual world.** When a virtual world rotates, the experience typically upsets people’s sense of stability, even when they control the rotation and the movement is subtle. Instead, consider using instantaneous directional changes during a quick fade-out.

**Consider giving people a stationary frame of reference.** It can be easier for people to handle visual movement when it’s contained within an area that doesn’t move. In contrast, if the entire surrounding area appears to move — for example, in a game that automatically moves a player through space — people can feel unwell.

**Avoid showing objects that oscillate in a sustained way.** In particular, you want to avoid showing an oscillation that has a frequency of around 0.2 Hz because people can be very sensitive to this frequency. If you need to show objects oscillating, aim to keep the amplitude low and consider making the content translucent.

### watchOS

SwiftUI provides a powerful and streamlined way to add motion to your app. If you need to use WatchKit to animate layout and appearance changes — or create animated image sequences — see <doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/WatchKit/WKInterfaceImage>.

> Note: All layout- and appearance-based animations automatically include built-in easing that plays at the start and end of the animation. You can’t turn off or customize easing.

**Cursors and presence:** The article doesn't cover them at all. It says nothing about how remote cursors are drawn, interpolated or animated.

**Smoothing remote updates:** The only related part is about preventing flicker when edits conflict:

- Your own edits show up right away, before the server confirms them.
- Without extra handling, older values that the server had already confirmed could briefly overwrite your newer, unconfirmed ones. The article calls this "flicker".
- To stop it, the client ignores any incoming server change that conflicts with a local property change the server hasn't confirmed yet. The idea is to "show the user our best prediction of what the eventually-consistent value will be."

One other visual edge case is reparenting cycles, where two objects are each made the other's parent. In that case the objects are briefly pulled out of the tree, and the object "temporarily disappears" until the server rejects the change.

The extra code attached below the page is a WebGPU ink simulation and isn't part of Figma's article. Its `ema` function smooths GPU timing stats, not remote updates.

The page only partly covers this. It gives the Android details but says almost nothing about Linux.

**Android:** Chrome 121 added support, on devices with "Android 12 and greater powered by Qualcomm and ARM GPUs."

**Linux:** There's no version number or timeline. The page only says "Linux and expanded support for existing platforms is coming soon."

**Not on the page:**
- Intel Gen12 or any other Intel GPU requirement
- Any flags for turning WebGPU on
- Any Linux driver or backend details, such as Vulkan on Linux

This search found the main sources on smoothing multiplayer cursors: Steve Ruiz's `perfect-cursors` library and Liveblocks' blog post on cursor animation. Nothing about PartyKit came up.

**perfect-cursors (Steve Ruiz / tldraw)**
- The [GitHub repo](https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-cursors) describes it as "Perfect interpolation for animated multiplayer cursors. Used in tldraw." You install it with `npm i perfect-cursors` and import it as `import { PerfectCursor } from "perfect-cursors"`. The latest release is 1.0.5 ([npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/perfect-cursors), [libraries.io](https://libraries.io/npm/perfect-cursors)).
- The problem it solves: "Updating the cursors' locations directly will cause cursors to 'jump' between points." For best results, you would animate while interpolating the cursors' locations based on a set of connected curves (e.g. a "spline"). The README demo is animating the cursor once position every 80 milliseconds using spline interpolation.
- How it works: "we create a 'spline' from the points that come in for that cursor, then play each 'segment' back as an animation in order." That's from Ruiz's [Dec 2021 tldraw cursor upgrade post](https://nitter.net/i/status/1473447802567020547).
- Background: in a [June 2021 thread](https://threadreaderapp.com/thread/1410173443832745988.html), Ruiz explained that regular tweens/duration-based animations won't work here because each new update will "redirect" the animation. By contrast, a spring animation will preserve its current momentum and velocity when beginning a new animation. That version used springs by @framer motion, live backend by @liveblocks.
- Ruiz has also pointed to [sshx](https://x.com/steveruizok/status/1721425763142951201), a collaborative terminal, as another app using perfect-cursors for those chefkiss spline-interpolated cursor positions.

**Liveblocks: "How to animate multiplayer cursors"** ([blog](https://liveblocks.io/blog/how-to-animate-multiplayer-cursors), by Chris Nicholas)
- The post compares three approaches: CSS transitions make for a quick-and-easy lightweight solution, whereas spring and spline animations result in a smoother experience.
- The catch with splines: the function waits to receive multiple points before rendering, so the cursor is slightly delayed. It recommends splines where accuracy is preferred and a little delay is acceptable. The easiest way to do this in React is with the perfect‑cursors library.
- The [HN discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31987713) suggested another method: save off all the mouse positions, and then send the latest batch every 100ms. The other side would then replay the exact positions, just delayed by 100ms.
- Nicholas [reshared the article in Feb 2026](https://x.com/ctnicholasdev/status/2018354238867591321), saying the techniques still apply.

Sources agree that `backdrop-filter` is one of the most expensive CSS effects. It re-blurs whatever is behind the element on every frame where that content changes, such as during scrolling. The cost goes up with the blur radius, the size of the area and the number of glass layers.

**Why it costs so much**
- The browser has to retain a separate GPU buffer for the area behind the element, because the filter has to read those pixels at composite time. One article suggests thinking of it as a *render-time image processing step*, not a paint effect.
- The Gaussian blur kernel has quadratic complexity relative to the radius. A GitHub issue makes the same point: blur cost grows with radius², and backdrop-filter pays it **per frame** whenever what's behind the layer changes (scrolling, chat streaming)
- One rendering guide gives rough GPU time per tile: Blur filter (10px): 5-10ms - Backdrop-filter: 10-20ms (requires background layer sampling)
- In one report, a 12 px blur on a full-viewport hero card on a mid-range Android device can drop scroll FPS by 15–25.

**Real cases**
- In one GitHub PR, the scroll jank was GPU paint, not main-thread work. The cause turned out to be **16 backdrop-filter surfaces**, the costly ones *inside the scrolling content*. Several of them sat on an **opaque** background (bg-[#f5f5f7]) — so in light mode they blurred pixels that were then painted over completely.
- Another project traced constant GPU load to large backdrop-filter radii on full-width glass surfaces (recomputed every frame whenever the backdrop changes), plus continuously running decorative animations. Integrated-GPU users were hit hardest.
- On iOS Safari, applying backdrop-filter to a position: fixed element causes severe scroll jank — the browser repaints the blurred area on every scroll frame.
- On Firefox, heavy backdrops can pull scrolling off the compositor thread, and there are long-standing open bugs around it.

**Mitigations**
- Keep the surface small: a 600 × 400 card is fine; a 100% × 100% full-screen blurred layer is the canonical mistake.
- Keep the radius low. Cap it at about 16px, because beyond that, the perceptual gain is small and the GPU cost grows super-linearly. Another source says to keep it under about 20px on large surfaces: a 24px blur on a chip is fine; on a full-width header it's a GPU tax on every scroll frame.
- Use three or four glass layers per viewport, maximum.
- Never animate the blur radius. Doing so forces full re-compositing per frame and drops phones to ~30fps. Keep the blur fixed and animate opacity instead.
- For sticky headers, use a near-opaque background without `backdrop-filter`. A semi-transparent background with no blur is the most robust choice

**From the earlier SVG filter search:** a full-page `feTurbulence` background caused scroll jank, and switching to a tiled `noise.webp` brought scrolling back to a smooth 120 FPS. That author notes that SVG filters and `backdrop-filter` both have render costs that often stay hidden until you test on high-refresh-rate screens or low-end devices.

A Fix-It Guide — Re:Form Sculpt Blog","url":"https://reformsculpt.com/blog/webgpu-not-working-fix"}]

Yes. Chrome 144 turns on WebGPU by default on Linux, but only for Intel Gen12 and newer GPUs, and it runs through Vulkan.

**Official source (Chrome for Developers, "What's New in WebGPU (Chrome 144)"):**
- The Chrome team is carefully rolling out WebGPU for Linux, starting with support for Intel Gen12+ GPUs but with a tentative plan to expand it to more devices (AMD, NVIDIA).
- How it works: WebGPU uses Vulkan and the rest of Chromium stays on OpenGL, exercising existing well known good code paths.
- Other Chrome 144 WebGPU changes listed: the WGSL subgroup_id and uniform_buffer_standard_layout extensions, faster writeBuffer/writeTexture, and Dawn updates.

**Later expansion (third-party sources):**
- Linux support followed in version 144 for Intel GPUs and was extended to NVIDIA GPUs in version 147.
- In more detail: Chrome ships WebGPU by default on Linux for Intel Gen12 and newer from Chrome 144, and for NVIDIA with driver 535.183.01 or newer under Wayland from Chrome 147.
- Everything else (AMD, older Intel, NVIDIA on X11) needs the flag stack the wiki lists: --enable-unsafe-webgpu --ozone-platform=x11 --use-angle=vulkan --enable-features=Vulkan,VulkanFromANGLE.
- The `--ozone-platform=x11` flag is there because, per one gist, Vulkan ANGLE isn't compatible with Wayland.

**Checking it:** open chrome://gpu (or edge://gpu) and look at the WebGPU line: "Hardware accelerated" means it works. WebGPU needs a working Vulkan driver, and on Linux that is where things usually go wrong.

**Out-of-date source:** testmuai.com (about 187 days old) still says Linux Chrome needs the `#enable-unsafe-webgpu` flag. That doesn't match the Chrome blog or the newer sources for Intel Gen12+ hardware.

**What it does:** perfect-cursors is an MIT-licensed library that makes remote cursors in multiplayer apps move smoothly even though their positions arrive only now and then. It's used in tldraw. Moving a cursor straight to each new position makes it "jump" between points. CSS transitions also fall short because updates don't arrive at exact intervals, so some animations never finish and others pause. The library fixes this by fitting a curve (a spline) through the incoming points and then playing each segment back as an animation, one after another ([Ruiz's tldraw post](https://nitter.net/i/status/1473447802567020547)). To use it, you create a `PerfectCursor` with a callback that runs on every frame, call `addPoint` each time a new position comes in, and call `dispose` to clean up.

**Interval and latency tradeoff:**
- **Interval:** The README says multiplayer services usually throttle updates to about one every 50–80 ms. Its demo sends a new point every 80 ms.
- **Tradeoff:** The movement looks very close to real motion, but the cursor runs one update behind. The README says it looks like it's updating "in real time" with a "one-update" delay. That's roughly 80 ms in the demo.
- **How it compares:** The [Liveblocks article](https://liveblocks.io/blog/how-to-animate-multiplayer-cursors) explains that splines lag slightly because they need several points before drawing anything. It suggests them when accuracy matters more than a small delay, and recommends perfect-cursors for React. In an [earlier thread](https://threadreaderapp.com/thread/1410173443832745988.html), Ruiz noted that springs avoid this wait because they keep their momentum when a new target arrives.

Sources: [GitHub repo](https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-cursors), [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/perfect-cursors)

The search found a fair amount on how Paper sets stroke width from drawing speed and its "no settings" approach. It found nothing on ink "bleed," such as how watercolor edges spread or pool. FiftyThree never seems to have published the engine's algorithms.

**Design approach (FiftyThree, [Core77 Design Awards 2013](https://designawards.core77.com/2013/recipients/paper-fiftythree/index.html))**
- FiftyThree says it chose not to copy real brushes: "Where everyone else tried to mimic realistic brushes and fell short, we took a different approach. Each of our tools is based around a key creative activity—sketching, drawing, writing, coloring, etc."
- Their custom-built Expressive Ink Engine is based on a handcrafted set of algorithms that allow for a range of expression from a single tool without requiring any settings.
- Paper took a focused 10-month process. Besides wireframes and prototypes, the team built its own tools, such as an in-app heads-up display for adjusting variables like gestures and lighting from within the development environment.

**Speed sets the width when there's no pressure input ([Made Mistakes, Michael Rose](https://mademistakes.com/mastering-paper/introduction-tool-guide/))**
- Width isn't controlled or set in a conventional sense. The speed at which you draw allows you to vary it. Each tool is slightly different in how speed affects it.
- Write (ink pen): its lines have heavier spots where a stroke stops or starts. Moving quickly through the whole stroke gives uniform lines. It has less variation in line width than the other tools.
- Pressure: a pressure-sensitive stylus like the Pogo Connect lets you make thinner lines. Other styli work only as "dumb" styli, so they make a mark but get no extras like pressure sensitivity. With FiftyThree's Pencil, you get a fatter stroke from the long side of the tip and a thin stroke from the tip itself ([Pencil review](https://mademistakes.com/mastering-paper/pencil-53-review/)).
- Marker (Outline): a single-width bold stroke that gets slightly more saturated where you go over an area more than once ([Hello Brio](https://www.hellobrio.com/blog/digital-drawing-paper-fiftythree)).

**Engine history**
- Version 1.3.1 rebuilt the Expressive Ink Engine on OpenGL for faster rendering ([9to5Mac](https://9to5mac.com/guides/paper-by-fiftythree/)). A later update advertised three times faster ink ([iMore](https://www.imore.com/paper-fiftythree-update-faster-ink-edge-edge-drawing-more)).
- Paper is now a WeTransfer product ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FiftyThree)).

**For comparison:** Inkscape's calligraphy pen has a published version of the same speed-to-width idea. Its thinning parameter runs from -100 to 100: zero means width doesn't depend on speed, positive values make faster strokes thinner, and negative values make them wider ([Scribd tutorial](https://www.scribd.com/document/368684353/Tutorial-Calligraphy)).

**Earlier searches:** The Think Kit results ([Medium, "The Intention Behind Think Kit"](https://medium.com/fiftythree-space-to-create/the-intention-behind-think-kit-6d79e7efd74b), [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2015/05/12/fiftythree-think-kit/), [The Next Web](https://thenextweb.com/news/fiftythree-debuts-think-kit-toolset-for-its-paper-ipad-app), [Georg Petschnigg's Tumblr](https://georgp.tumblr.com/post/118778676766/we-launched-our-most-advanced-foray-into-design), [iPhone J.D.](https://www.iphonejd.com/iphone_jd/2012/04/review-paper-fiftythree-ipad.html), [Archinect](https://archinect.com/news/article/104799766/archinect-test-drives-fiftythree-s-pencil-and-paper-app-for-ipad), [Core77](https://www.core77.com/posts/22101/We-love-Paper-by-FiftyThree-New-Sketching-App-for-iPad)) say Think Kit's Intention Engine controls the Ink Engine's settings and replays strokes. I ran the search. Most results are about f.lux itself, not about designing a UI theme that follows the time of day. The one closest to UI design is a Hacker News thread.

**How f.lux handles the day (official docs)**
- f.lux has three phases. Daytime is whenever the sun is up in your location. Sunset is when the sun has set, but you are awake. If you are an early riser, this is also your pre-sunrise morning setting. A later bedtime phase is around the time you would start feeling sleepy, we do a little more, helping you get to bed on time. We've even tried to time this second phase with your body's natural release of melatonin. ([f.lux for Mac update](https://justgetflux.com/news/pages/mac/))
- Default values: By default, f.lux is at 6500K during the daytime, and does not change your screen's color. With the Classic preset, at sunset, f.lux will fade to 3400K, and turn off at sunrise. ([macOS quickstart](https://justgetflux.com/news/pages/macquickstart/))
- Transition speed: with "Fast transitions" on, it does a 20 second fade at sunrise and sunset. When unchecked, f.lux changes gradually over one hour. One fix: If you woke up your laptop late in the day, f.lux used to do a very slow transition (as if you were "used to" the orange color). Now it transitions quickly to daylight instead.
- Theme switching: one option uses the normal theme during the day and switches to dark theme (dock and menu bar) each night at sunset.
- Its interface shows you a visualization of your day, and the app displays your current solar time and counts down to sunrise or sunset right in its interface. ([MakeUseOf](https://www.makeuseof.com/screen-adjusts-to-rooms-light-automatically/))
- f.lux's developer says the product's main goal is helping people control when they sleep and wake: every decision we make (e.g., which controls to put in the interface) is based on that goal. ([f.lux forum](https://forum.justgetflux.com/topic/4185/how-do-i-tell-f-lux-what-my-bedtime-is))

**Hacker News: "Dark mode by local sunlight (2021)"** ([thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45799949), about ctnicholas.dev)
- One commenter wants the switch to go unnoticed: It would be great if the transition to dark mode be invisible. Like after locking laptop's screen, not in the process of work.
- Another made a set of themes across several apps that change with time of day: day, late afternoon/evening, sunset/twilight, night, post-midnight. At night, it smoothly fades the light panels into a display that represents a angle compressed sky projection of the stars.
- A drawback for people far from the equator: for folks living in the far north, it actually makes seasonal changes so much worse.

**Related**
- Night Shift is a built in software feature of iOS and macOS. The feature when set to enable at sunset and disable at sunrise relies on the user's approximate location to determine the time of sunset and sunrise. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Shift_(software)))

- **Suggested fix:** A speed setting with three choices: off, normal and fast.

The replies from unrealapex and Miodec only talk about the result-screen request and don't mention the caret. The extra material you included, on Paper by FiftyThree and perfect-cursors, isn't about Monkeytype, so I left it out.

Both commenters dislike Word's animated cursor. Nobody in the thread defends it.

**GordonS (distraction)**
- Says the gliding cursor, which animates even while you type, is "_really_ off-putting."
- Turning off animations in Windows gets rid of it. But that setting "is reverted" after some Windows updates.

**Stratoscope (latency, bad design)**
- "Yes, that cursor animation is just awful."
- Calls it a "laggy animation" put on top of what should be an instant action, like a keypress or arrow key, and says "It's simply a ridiculous idea."
- Word's own "Provide feedback with animation" option doesn't help: "turning off this checkbox does nothing!" The only fix is the Windows-wide setting.
- Also complains about Excel, which slides the selection border from the old cell to the one you clicked. Unlike Word, Excel's own setting does turn it off.

The extra material attached to your message (FiftyThree's Paper and the perfect-cursors library) is about different topics, so I didn't use it here.

Here are the Animation and Performance rules from the Vercel Web Interface Guidelines, quoted as written. One rule was longer than 125 characters, so I split it into two quotes.

**Motion rules**

- "Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` (provide reduced variant or disable)"
- "Animate `transform`/`opacity` only (compositor-friendly)"
- "Never `transition: all`—list properties explicitly"
- "Set correct `transform-origin`"
- "SVG: transforms on `<g>` wrapper with `transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center`"
- "Animations interruptible—respond to user input mid-animation"
- "Autoplay motion >5 seconds alongside other content needs pause, stop, or hide controls"
- "Muted decorative loops must stop under `prefers-reduced-motion`"

**Performance rules**

- "Large lists (>50 items): virtualize (`virtua`, `content-visibility: auto`)"
- "No layout reads in render (`getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetHeight`, `offsetWidth`, `scrollTop`)"
- "Batch DOM reads/writes; avoid interleaving"
- "Prefer uncontrolled inputs; controlled inputs must be cheap per keystroke"
- "Add `<link rel="preconnect">` for CDN/asset domains"
- "Critical fonts: `<link rel="preload" as="font">` with `font-display: swap`"

Chrome turns WebGPU on by default on Linux only for some GPUs: Intel Gen12 and newer since Chrome 144, and recent NVIDIA under Wayland since Chrome 147. Everything else still needs flags.

**Rollout by version:**
- Linux support followed in version 144 for Intel GPUs and was extended to NVIDIA GPUs in version 147.
- In more detail, Chrome ships WebGPU by default on Linux for Intel Gen12 and newer from Chrome 144, and for NVIDIA with driver 535.183.01 or newer under Wayland from Chrome 147.
- Earlier results included the official Chrome blog post ["What's New in WebGPU (Chrome 144)"](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-webgpu-144). It says the rollout starts with Intel Gen12+ and that the team tentatively plans to add AMD and NVIDIA later. WebGPU runs on Vulkan while the rest of Chromium stays on OpenGL. I couldn't find a Chrome release note confirming the NVIDIA step in Chrome 147. That claim comes only from Wikipedia and a third-party guide.
- Background: the first release, in Chrome 113, covered ChromeOS devices with Vulkan support, Windows devices with Direct3D 12 support, and macOS. Linux and Android were promised "soon."

**Hardware that still needs flags:**
- Everything else (AMD, older Intel, NVIDIA on X11) needs the flag stack the wiki lists: --enable-unsafe-webgpu --ozone-platform=x11 --use-angle=vulkan --enable-features=Vulkan,VulkanFromANGLE.
- Because WebGPU runs on Vulkan while the rest of the browser stays on OpenGL, the rollout is gated per GPU family.
- A simpler route through chrome://flags: turn on chrome://flags/#enable-unsafe-webgpu, then on Linux also turn on chrome://flags/#enable-vulkan, and restart Chrome. To check it worked, open chrome://gpu and look for the line "WebGPU: Hardware accelerated".

**Current Chrome versions:** Chrome 156.0.8078.47 has been the stable Linux release since 20 October 2026, and 157 is in preview.

**Firefox:** as of October 2026, WebGPU isn't on by default in regular Firefox on Linux. It's only on by default in Firefox Nightly.

**Source to be careful with:** testmuai.com (from an earlier search, about 187 days old) still says Linux Chrome always needs the flag. That's out of date for Intel Gen12+ and newer NVIDIA hardware.

I couldn't find a Raycast blog post about skipping open/close animation, and the exact phrase "feels instant" didn't come up anywhere. The idea comes from Emil Kowalski's essay, which uses Raycast as its example.

**Main source: Emil Kowalski, ["You Don't Need Animations"](https://emilkowal.ski/ui/you-dont-need-animations)**
- His key point: "I use Raycast hundreds of times a day. If it animated every time I opened it, it would be very annoying. But there's no animation at all. That's the optimal experience."
- He says the reason is that he opens Raycast with a clear goal in mind and doesn't expect or need to be "delighted".
- On keyboard actions, he writes that because they may be repeated hundreds of times a day, an animation would make them feel slow, delayed, and disconnected from the user's actions. You should never animate them.
- On speed, he notes that a 180ms dropdown animation feels more responsive than a 400ms one. He also says that once one tooltip is open, hovering over other tooltips should open them with no delay and no animation.

**The same rule in Emil's agent skills**
- [emil-design-eng on Flowy](https://www.flowy.sh/listings/emilkowalski-skills/skills/emil-design-eng) has a table based on how often something is used: "100+ times/day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle) | No animation. Ever." Things used tens of times a day, like hovers, should have animation removed or cut way down. Things used occasionally, like modals, get standard animation. Things seen rarely can add delight.
- [The animate skill on ui-skills.com](https://www.ui-skills.com/skills/emilkowalski/animate) says: "Keyboard-initiated actions are a disqualifier, not a judgment call. Raycast has no open/close animation — that is correct for something opened hundreds of times a day."

**Raycast's own blog, [A Technical Deep Dive Into the New Raycast](https://www.raycast.com/blog/a-technical-deep-dive-into-the-new-raycast) (May 2026)**
- This post is about feeling native rather than about having no animation. Their test is whether someone using Raycast without knowing what it's built with would think it's a regular Mac app. If anything feels off – a wrong animation, a hover state that doesn't belong – they haven't done their job.
- They also say there is no flickering when views appear or transition, which is a common tell in web apps.
- One WebKit issue they had to fix: WebKit throttles requestAnimationFrame, CSS animations, and timers when it considers the view invisible, which breaks a launcher that's constantly shown and hidden. A translation is on [Lucky Snail](https://luckysnail.cn/en/posts/deep-dive-new-raycast-technical-details).

**Raycast's marketing site (not the app)**
- These are unofficial third-party breakdowns. [webdesignhot's DESIGN.md](https://www.webdesignhot.com/design.md/raycast/) lists hover transitions at about 100ms. [oh-my-design](https://oh-my-design.kr/design-systems/raycast) says no official source consulted publishes a motion scale.

The new search confirms the expanded context. Jakob Nielsen's NN/g article sets three response time limits: 0.1 seconds, 1 second and 10 seconds.

**Main source:** ["Response Times: The 3 Important Limits"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/) by Jakob Nielsen. The [NN/g response-time topic page](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/response-time/) dates it January 1, 1993. The article says there are 3 main time limits (which are determined by human perceptual abilities) to keep in mind when optimizing web and application performance. It is a chapter 5 excerpt from Nielsen's 1993 book *Usability Engineering*.

**The three limits** (as quoted in [Let's Decode AI](https://letsdecodeai.com/insights/putting-a-model-behind-an-interface)):
- 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously.
- 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted, even though the user will notice the delay.
- 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.
- Between 0.1 and 1 second, no special feedback is necessary, but the user does lose the feeling of operating directly on the data ([Oatsnotes](https://oatsnotes.com/posts/response-time-limits.html)).

**Feedback guidance in the same article:**
- In cases where the computer cannot provide fairly immediate response, continuous feedback should be provided to the user in form of a percent-done indicator [Myers 1985].
- Feedback during the delay is especially important if the response time is likely to be highly variable, since users will then not know what to expect.
- The article says the response time guidelines for web-based applications are the same as for all other applications.

**Related NN/g material:**
- A video version, "The 3 Response Time Limits in Interaction Design" (October 25, 2019).
- A September 2020 video, "Mask Interaction Delays with Progress Indicators." Its advice: for slow responses, indicate that the wait time will soon be over by showing an animation. For longer delays use a percent-done indicator.
- ["The Need for Speed" (1997)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/the-need-for-speed-1997/) says the minimum goal for response times should therefore be to get pages to users in no more than ten seconds.
- ["Powers of 10: Time Scales in User Experience"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/powers-of-10-time-scales-in-ux/) (2009) came up in the earlier search.

**Origins:** The limits are based on response-time limits established by Miller, 1968 and further explored by Nielsen ([Pratt IxD](https://ixd.prattsi.org/2015/04/response-time-is-speed-the-ultimate-usability-metric/)). The earlier results also cited Card and colleagues (1991), per [Boostbery](https://boostbery.com/insights/why-your-brain-hates-slow-websites-the-psychology-of-page-speed/).

**Still not found:** NN/g's separate progress-indicators article, sometimes cited for "spinners for about 2–10 seconds, percent-done for over 10 seconds." One citing page mentions a related NN/g title, "Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable". Searching that title directly should find it.

**Other sources:** These results also had [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/nielsen-norman-response-times-0-1-1-10-seconds-user-experience/), [Miris](https://www.miris.com/blog/you-wouldnt-download-a-movie-before-watching-it), [Jacob Medley](https://jacobmedley.com/musings/exploring-response-times-in-interaction-design/) and [Android Dev Social](https://androiddev.social/@rolgalan/113556707454352297). The earlier results included [Hello Retail](https://helloretail.com/en/blog/2026-10-09-fast-site-search-ecommerce/), [UX Collective](https://uxdesign.cc/the-waiting-problem-in-ai-products-e7c11fd5a825?gi=226235e5daa0), [WebYes](https://www.webyes.com/blogs/good-website-response-time/) and [Global Bridge Labs](https://globalbridgelabs.co.uk/blogs/how-long-visitors-wait-for-website).

The other context you sent (Apple's Motion guidelines and WebGPU browser support) has nothing to do with this search. Its sources were [Apple HIG Motion](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md), the [older HIG Motion page](https://developers.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/foundations/motion), [Use Your Loaf](https://useyourloaf.com/blog/reducing-motion-of-animations/), [Uxcel](https://uxcel.com/lessons/accessibility-inclusion-standards-812), [Wikipedia: WebGPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebGPU), [web.dev](https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers), [Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/webgpu/overview) and [Cinevva](https://app.cinevva.com/guides/webgl-webgpu-not-supported-fix).

I found plenty of practitioner guidance on AI loading, thinking and streaming states. However, no page from Shape of AI (shapeof.ai) came up, so search for it by name if you need its wording.

**What the sources agree on**
- **Stream when you can, otherwise show steps.** A ten-second spinner makes people think the app has frozen. Streaming text, where words appear as they are generated, is the standard answer because users can start reading while the model is still working. When streaming is not possible, use step-by-step progress messages: "Reading your document," then "Extracting key figures," then "Formatting the summary." ([UX Planet](https://agency.uxplanet.org/blog/ai-ux-patterns/))
- **Don't claim to know the finish time.** The goal is to communicate request progress, streaming readiness, and intermediate AI work without pretending to know the exact finish time. A status label explains whether the model is thinking, retrieving, or generating. ([uxpatterns.dev](https://uxpatterns.dev/patterns/ai-intelligence/ai-loading-states))
- **Label states honestly.** Use Thinking, Reasoning, or Searching the web instead of vague terms like Working on it. Suggested targets include first token starts streaming within 800ms of submit, or a queued state is shown, plus a visible Stop button. ([Setproduct](https://www.setproduct.com/blog/ai-chat-interface-ui-design))
- **Use different treatments as the wait grows.** Phase 2 (500ms-2s): subtle typing indicator. Dots, cursor, or "Thinking..." label. No progress bar, since you cannot estimate LLM completion time accurately. Phase 3 (2-5s): contextual progress message. Phase 4 (5s+): step progress with cancel option "Checked 3 of 5 sources..." plus a cancel button. Tool calls count as a 5th state with a specific label. ([curiousengineers.in](https://curiousengineers.in/blog/ai-ux-patterns))
- **Keep the steps collapsed but available.** Streaming answers "Is anything happening?" Progress steps answer "What kind of work is happening?" Show them in collapsible steps and keep it quiet by default, available on demand. ([AI UX Playground guide](https://aiuxplayground.com/guides/designing-better-ai-chat-part-1))
- **Don't fake progress.** One anti-pattern listed is streaming fake progress while the model has not started. ([AI UX Playground, Streaming](https://aiuxplayground.com/pattern/streaming/))
- **The Claude-style reasoning display.** The recommended approach is hidden by default, expandable on demand, structured bullets when expanded, time counter or progress indicator, clear "done" state. For multi-step work: show current step + total steps, mark completed steps visually. ([ai-loading-ux skill](https://atskills.one/shipshitdev/ai-loading-ux))
- **Examples from real products.** Claude's extended thinking mode shows "Thinking for N seconds" with a live counter, then transitions into the answer stream. The article separates token streaming from phase-based streaming, which surfaces higher-level status events (thinking, searching, writing) between or alongside token output. ([AYDesign](https://www.aydesign.ai/blog/ai-streaming-response-ui-patterns-2026))
- **Accessibility.** Streaming text is hard for screen readers, which may read each new word separately or lose their place.
- **A number to treat with caution.** [Thrive with AI](https://www.thrivewithai.live/blog/ai-ux-design-patterns-that-work) gives a staged-label timing table and claims that streaming reduces perceived wait time by 87%. It cites no source for that figure.

I searched once. I found nothing that directly criticizes hold-to-confirm for destructive actions or maps it to a specific WCAG criterion. The results do cover the timing and motor-control issues that are relevant.

**Direct criticism of press-and-hold (closest match)**
- Buttondown "Access-Ability" uses press-and-hold "show password" as its example. It says press-and-hold is allowed under WCAG; however, it still forces timing precision and fine motor control. Its suggested fix is a persistent toggle, which removes the timing burden that disproportionately affects blind and motor-limited users. It treats this as a usability problem, not a WCAG failure.

**WCAG 2.5 (Input Modalities) context**
- Pointer cancellation (2.5.2): the action shouldn't be finalized until you release your finger, which is the up event. If you change your mind while holding down, you should be able to move your finger away and not trigger anything. Silktide says this prevents accidental clicks and taps, especially for users with motor impairments. A hold that fires on a timer while the finger is still down works differently, so it's worth checking against 2.5.2.
- Dragging (2.5.7) is a related case: it's a barrier for users with motor impairments who can't easily click, hold, move, and release at the right spot. WCAG 2.2 requires an equivalent option that works with a simple click or tap. WCAG Pros adds that a keyboard alternative alone isn't enough, because users must have a single pointer alternative, such as a button or a menu, that they can operate with simple taps. It also notes that tremor conditions make it extremely difficult to maintain steady pressure on a mouse button or screen.

**Timing (2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, Level A)**
- The accessibility.build page lists who is affected: Switch access, eye-gaze, and one-handed or tremor-affected typing all slow input. It's about session and form timeouts, though, not hold durations.

**My own reading (not from these sources, please verify against the W3C Understanding docs):** SC 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures covers multipoint and path-based gestures. A stationary single-pointer long press probably isn't covered by it. So the strongest arguments are 2.5.2, the general advice to offer a single-tap alternative, and usability concerns, rather than a clear WCAG failure.

**From earlier searches (still relevant)**
- Two usability problems came up: waiting through a delay on every item when deleting many in a row, and users not realizing they have to hold instead of click. OlegWock also says the pattern probably won't replace GitHub-style typed confirmation if you care about accessibility.
- Common fixes in component libraries: holding Space/Enter, a single activation for screen readers (Beste UI, velvet-ui's `.accessibilityAction`), and a tap-to-confirm-dialog fallback (Lepid's `confirmOnKeyboardTap`). Hold durations ranged from about 300 ms to 2 s.

## Animation values from Emil Kowalski's STANDARDS.md

**Cubic-bezier curves.** The file says CSS's built-in easings aren't strong enough and gives these custom curves:
- `"--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);"`, labeled as a "strong ease-out for UI"
- `"--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1);"`, for "on-screen movement." The WAAPI example in the file uses this curve again.
- `"--ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);"`, described as an "iOS-like drawer curve (Ionic)"

**Scale for entering elements.**
- "Never `scale(0)`."
- "Start from `scale(0.9–0.97)` + `opacity: 0`."
- The reason given: "Nothing in the real world appears from nothing."
- For press feedback, which isn't an entry animation, it uses `"transform: scale(0.97)"` on `:active`.

**Ease-in rule.**
- "Never `ease-in` on UI."
- "It starts slow, delaying the exact moment the user is watching."
- "`ease-out` at 200ms _feels_ faster than `ease-in` at 200ms."

**Other sources.** None of the earlier search results give exact easing values. The Arc and Things 3 results don't include curves or spring settings. You asked me to list those sources anyway:
- **Web animation and accessibility:** [Vercel Web Interface Guidelines](https://vercel.com/design/guidelines), [A List Apart: Designing Safer Web Animation](https://alistapart.com/article/designing-safer-web-animation-for-motion-sensitivity/), [ALA Issue 428](https://alistapart.com/issue/428/), [WCAG 2.1 #18](https://github.com/w3c/wcag21/issues/18), [Tuts+](https://webdesign.tutsplus.com/a-guide-to-creating-accessible-animations--cms-32038t), [neurodiversity.design](https://neurodiversity.design/principles/animations/), [Ben Myers](https://benmyers.dev/encyclopedia/reduced-motion/), [Matuzović](https://matuzo.at/blog/reading-recommendations-animation-on-the-web-and-vestibular-disorders)
- **Apple:** [Apple HIG Motion](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md), [older HIG URL](https://developers.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/foundations/motion), [Use Your Loaf](https://useyourloaf.com/blog/reducing-motion-of-animations/), [Uxcel](https://uxcel.com/lessons/accessibility-inclusion-standards-812), [WWDC18 Designing Fluid Interfaces](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2018/803/)
- **Teenage Engineering OP-1:** [Teenage Engineering](https://teenage.engineering/products/op-1/original/overview), [Soundtech](https://www.soundtech.co.uk/musicians-blog/our-guide-to-the-teenage-engineering-op-1.html), [CDM](https://cdm.link/teenage-engineerings-op-1-instrument-hands-on-videos-why-its-different/), [Blake Crosley](https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering), [The Synth Source](https://thesynthsource.com/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable/), [designboom](https://www.designboom.com/technology/teenage-engineering-op-1-portable-synthesizer/), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering_OP-1)
- **Other design references:** [Figma Multiplayer](https://www.figma.com/blog/multiplayer-editing-in-figma/), [Learn UI: Invisible Details](https://learn-ui.com/chapters/invisible-details)

# Raycast 2.0: animation, native feel, and speed

**Animation**
- Polish standard: "If anything feels off – a wrong animation, a hover state that doesn't belong, a popover that clips at the window edge"
- WebKit problem: it "throttles `requestAnimationFrame`, CSS animations, and timers when it thinks a view isn't visible."
- Resizing: "WebKit suspends drawing during animated window resizes, which caused visible stuttering." They fixed it by using implicit Core Animation instead.
- Transitions: "No flickering when views appear or transition."
- Frame rate: they use runtime WebKit flags to "unlock the 60 FPS cap."

**Feeling native**
- The test: would someone "think it's a regular Mac app?"
- Their framing: "We're a native app that uses web for its UI."
- Focus: "It's about making things behave right."
- Conventions: "No `cursor: pointer` on interactive controls. Desktop apps don't do this." Popovers and tooltips are real native windows, and on Tahoe the app uses Liquid Glass.

**Speed and latency**
- Core challenge: "The hard part was making it feel right."
- File indexer: built to "scan entire hard drives within seconds."
- Windows opening: they make sure the WebView "has finished drawing before the window becomes visible."
- Text: in rich text rendering, "WebKit really shines."
- Trade-off: inactive windows are now closed down, so "there's a short delay when you open them cold." Grace periods are planned to keep recently used windows ready.
- Development: "UI changes show up in under a second" thanks to hot reloading.

content.text:
I've written the report below with a source URL on each bullet. Some details I couldn't confirm are flagged inline and collected in the last section.

## Research report: interaction motion for Twyne

### 1. Game feel and juice applied to productivity UI
- **Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho, GDC 2012).** They take a plain Breakout and keep the rules fixed. They then add layers in order: colour, tweening and easing, squash and stretch, sound, particles, screen shake, then faces. Takeaway: feedback comes in layers on top of rules that don't change, so juice is presentation and never changes outcomes. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose
- **Screen shake causes motion sickness.** Later write-ups say "a shake should be a punch, not an earthquake." Shake a stamp, never the viewport. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose (Nijman's "Art of Screenshake" talk covers the same ground)
- **Emil Kowalski: animation budget scales with how often an action happens.** Rules from his STANDARDS.md:
  - Used 100+ times a day: no animation.
  - Used tens of times a day: remove or minimise.
  - Occasional (modals, toasts): a standard animation.
  - Rare (onboarding, celebrations): delight is allowed.
  - Keyboard-triggered actions are never animated. Raycast is his example.
  https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/blob/main/skills/review-animations/STANDARDS.md
- **Kowalski's numbers.**
  - UI animations stay under 300ms. 200ms is the default.
  - Press feedback is 100–160ms, for example `transform 160ms ease-out` with scale 0.97.
  - Tooltips take 125ms, and every tooltip after the first shows instantly.
  - Drawers take about 500ms with `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`.
  - Stagger items by 30–80ms.
  - Use ease-out for entering elements and avoid ease-in, which feels slow.
  - Use blur (around 2px) only as a last resort to smooth a crossfade.
  https://emilkowal.ski/ui/7-practical-animation-tips
- **Rauno Freiberg, "Invisible details of interaction design".**
  - Motion should be interruptible: you can reverse it mid-gesture and never have to wait for it to finish.
  - Thrown objects keep their momentum, and bounce matches how heavy the object should feel.
  - A threshold commits an action. Before the threshold, the response tracks the input.
  - "Fidgetability" means small satisfying responses invite people to repeat them.
  - Scroll stays with the pane where it started.
  Takeaway: margin notes and stamps should be draggable and reversible before they commit. https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design
- **Linear's timing.** This comes from a third-party reading of Linear's stylesheet, not from Linear itself. Highlights fade in over 0s and out over 0.15s. The quick, regular and slow transitions are 0.1s, 0.25s and 0.35s. Popovers appear instantly and fade out on dismiss. Width, height and margin are never animated. Takeaway: appear instantly, leave softly. https://performance.dev/how-is-linear-so-fast-a-technical-breakdown
- **Raycast's bar is "feeling native".** Their deep dive lists: no flicker when views appear, no `cursor: pointer` on controls, and the WebView finishes drawing before the window is shown. https://www.raycast.com/blog/a-technical-deep-dive-into-the-new-raycast
- **Apple HIG.** Avoid motion on UI interactions people repeat often. Avoid oscillation near 0.2 Hz (one cycle every five seconds); if something must oscillate, keep the amplitude low and the content translucent. This matters for any "breathing" idle state. https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion
- **Vercel interface guidelines.**
  - Animate only `transform` and `opacity`, and never use `transition: all`.
  - Every animation must be interruptible.
  - Motion that autoplays for more than 5 seconds needs a pause control.
  - Decorative loops stop under reduced motion.
  - Per-keystroke work must stay cheap.
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md

### 2. Editors with a distinctive typing, caret or scroll feel
- **Word's gliding caret (since Office 2013) is widely disliked.**
  - On Hacker News: "that cursor animation is just awful… laggy animation on top of what should be instant."
  - Word's own "Provide feedback with animation" checkbox doesn't turn it off. The only fixes are the Windows-wide animation setting (which some Windows updates turn back on) or the `DisableAnimations` registry value.
  Takeaway: never delay the caret on a keypress. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19686799
- **VS Code keeps the caret instant while typing.** `editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation` has the values off, explicit and on. "explicit" animates only when you jump with a click or navigation, not while typing. Adopt that split. https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332
- **Monkeytype** has `smoothCaret: off | slow | medium | fast`, and the speed setting came from users saying the glide was too slow. Typing-test users accept a smooth caret only when it is fast and optional. Source for the options: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype (packages/schemas/src/configs.ts). Source for the complaint: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248
- **iA Writer's Focus Mode** dims everything except the current sentence or paragraph, and Typewriter Mode keeps the current line vertically centred. Both are toggles, and the dimming is a colour change, not movement. https://ia.net/writer/support/editor/focus-mode
- **Ulysses, Typora, Obsidian, Bear.**
  - Ulysses' typewriter mode, with a configurable line position and a line highlight, is a fan favourite.
  - Typora has Focus (F8) and Typewriter (F9) modes.
  - Obsidian gets the same through the obsidian-typewriter-mode plugin, which offers line position as a percentage, a highlight style and paragraph dimming.
  - Bear users still have an open feature request for typewriter mode.
  Takeaway: writers value stillness and a predictable eye line more than motion. Unverified: Ulysses' exact options, because its help page now redirects.
- **Paper by FiftyThree (now WeTransfer)** drew stroke width from drawing speed rather than pressure, on a custom OpenGL engine; a later update advertised three-times-faster ink. A strong precedent for ink whose physics comes from speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FiftyThree
- **Teenage Engineering's OP-1** gives each mode its own colour and animated graphic, so the playful visuals tell you which mode you are in. https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering
- **Not verified:** Craft's and Hemingway's motion. Hemingway uses static colour highlights only.

### 3. Ink, paper and letterpress on the web
- **SVG filter recipes for type (Carmen Ansio).**
  - Ink gain: `feMorphology dilate`, then `feFlood`, then `feComposite in`.
  - Rough, bled edges: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap`. `fractalNoise` gives softer edges than `turbulence`.
  - Pitfalls: turbulence, displacement and lighting are the expensive primitives. Defs inside a `display:none` SVG are dropped in Chromium. Set `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"`. CSS cannot animate filter primitive attributes, so drive changes from JS with requestAnimationFrame and an IntersectionObserver.
  https://www.carmenansio.com/articles/svg-filters-on-type/
- **SVG filter performance.**
  - Keep the filter region tight. `feTurbulence` is unbounded and defaults to a region of 120%.
  - Never animate transform on a filtered element, because the filter is recomputed every frame.
  - Pre-render the result to a bitmap.
  - CSS filter functions are much cheaper than SVG filters.
  Rule for Twyne: never put a live filter on the editor surface. Use filters only on small, short-lived elements such as a stamp. https://tympanus.net/codrops/2019/02/19/svg-filter-effects-creating-texture-with-feturbulence/
- **Paper grain.** Generate the texture once (feTurbulence or a shader) and cache it as a tiled background. Lighting by a moving light is best done as a fragment shader on a small canvas behind the text, at half or quarter resolution, re-rendered only when the light moves. I found no authoritative procedural paper shader; three.js normal-map approaches exist. https://discourse.threejs.org/t/distorted-grainy-material-due-to-a-normal-map/72599
- **Risograph and halftone.** Codrops has a risograph grain tutorial. glsl-halftone provides rotated dot grids. Mis-registration is a UV offset per spot-ink layer, which suits two inks, vermilion and cobalt.
  - https://tympanus.net/codrops/2022/03/07/creating-a-risograph-grain-light-effect-in-three-js/
  - https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone
- **Letterpress deboss in CSS** is a pair of `text-shadow` layers: light offset down, dark offset up. Animating the pair fakes a moving light. Note that `text-shadow` does not render on `background-clip:text`.
- **`backdrop-filter`** is costly inside scrolling content. I found no benchmark. Avoid it over the manuscript.

### 4. Browser APIs (verified November 2026)
- **CSS Custom Highlight API.** Baseline Newly Available since 2026-03-24 (Chrome 105, Safari 17.2, Firefox 149).
  - Allowed properties: `color`, `background-color`, `text-decoration*`, `text-shadow`, `-webkit-text-stroke/fill`.
  - `background-image` is ignored.
  - There are no transitions or animations today. On 2026-10-30 the CSSWG resolved that highlights should get opacity and that animations and transitions should be allowed. That is spec intent and is not shipped.
  - To animate now, swap highlight names or change registered ranges from JS.
  - Sources: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::highlight and https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/14613
- **Same-document View Transitions.** Baseline Newly Available since 2025-10-14, Firefox 144 last. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/view-transitions/
- **Scroll-driven animations.** Baseline Newly Available since 2026-10-27 (Chrome 115, Safari 26, Firefox 159). Older articles saying Firefox needs a flag are out of date. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/scroll-driven-animations/
- **`@property`.** Baseline since 2024-07 (Firefox 128 last). Safe for animated gradients and ink-fill progress. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/registered-custom-properties/
- **`linear()` easing.** Widely Available since 2026-06. Safe for spring curves in pure CSS. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/linear-easing/
- **Popover** is Baseline since 2025-01 and **`@starting-style`** since 2024-08. I found no separate support data for `popover=hint`.
  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/popover/
  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/starting-style/
- **`interpolate-size`** ships in Chromium only (129+). Firefox and Safari have not shipped it. Gate it with `@supports`. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/interpolate-size/
- **WebGPU.**
  - Chrome 113+ on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS. Android ships too; I didn't confirm the version.
  - Firefox 141 on Windows, and Firefox 145 on Apple Silicon macOS Tahoe.
  - Safari 26.
  - Linux Chrome is a gradual rollout on Vulkan, and Linux Firefox is Nightly only.
  - WebGL2 stays the default for ambient shaders, with WebGPU as an optional upgrade.
  - https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers
  - https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-webgpu-144 (I could not confirm the exact Linux GPU list.)

### 5. Motion that communicates consequence and trust
- **Undo beats "are you sure?"** People click through repeated warnings out of habit (Raskin). Gmail's Undo Send holds the message 5–30s. Use a visible delayed commit for "send to AI" or "publish". Keep heavy friction, like typing the item's name as GitHub does, for permanent destructive actions only. https://alistapart.com/article/neveruseawarning/
- **Hold-to-confirm.** Timings in component libraries range from 300ms to 2s. It is hard for people with tremor, so provide a single-activation path for keyboard and screen readers, and let releasing early cancel cleanly. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pointer-cancellation.html
- **Disabled-with-reason.** Use `aria-disabled` rather than `disabled` so the control stays focusable, and explain why it is disabled. This fits out-of-credits and rate-limited states.
  - https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2021/08/frustrating-design-patterns-disabled-buttons/
  - https://uxdesign.cc/never-ever-disable-buttons-requirements-for-an-accessible-solution-acaf9c5191f9
- **Response-time limits (NN/g).**
  - Under 0.1s feels instant and needs no feedback.
  - About 1s keeps the user's train of thought; a subtle indicator helps.
  - Over about 10s needs real progress, such as percent done.
  Map AI waits onto these bands. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/
- **AI thinking states.**
  - Accepted patterns: show the current step and total steps, an elapsed counter ("Thinking for N s"), steps that collapse, and a clear "done" state.
  - Anti-pattern: fake progress shown before the model has started.
  - Text shimmer is now a generic AI cliché.
  - A stronger fit for Twyne is to show what an editor is reading, for example a marker moving through the paragraphs it has consumed.
  - Source: https://panelui.dev/docs/ai-components/shimmer, a component library. I found no authoritative critique of shimmer.

### 6. Ambient life and accessibility
- **Smooth remote cursors.** Fit a spline through position updates (about every 50–80ms) instead of using CSS transitions, which never finish when updates arrive irregularly. This is perfect-cursors, used in tldraw. Use it for any AI-editor presence marker. https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-cursors
- **Figma shows your own edits before the server confirms them** and ignores conflicting incoming changes until then, to avoid flicker. The same applies to local versus synced state. https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/
- **WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA).** Motion triggered by interaction must be possible to disable unless it is essential. Colour, blur and opacity changes don't count as motion, so a reduced-motion mode can keep fades and ink-colour shifts. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html
- **Vestibular triggers.** Parallax, scroll-jacking, zoom, spinning, and large or full-screen motion. Never use parallax or scroll-linked movement in the manuscript; scroll-driven effects belong in the margin or chrome only. https://alistapart.com/article/designing-safer-web-animation-for-motion-sensitivity/
- **Opt in to motion.** Josh Comeau and Ben Myers suggest motion only under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, plus an in-app override. https://benmyers.dev/encyclopedia/reduced-motion/
- **Time-of-day lighting.** Precedents are f.lux, Night Shift and dark mode by local sunlight (Hacker News, 2021). Change it slowly, never in steps, and keep text contrast fixed.

### What I couldn't verify
- Ulysses' exact typewriter-mode options (its help page redirected).
- Craft's motion behaviour.
- The exact GPU list for Chrome's WebGPU rollout on Linux.
- Kowalski's ease-out curve values other than the drawer curve.
- Linear's numbers are third-party, not from Linear.
- Apple HIG wording on "let people cancel" (not seen in the text I fetched).
- No benchmark for the cost of `backdrop-filter`.

### 10 gaps that fit a literary editor with AI editors
1. **A caret that never glides on a keystroke** but leaves a brief wet-ink fade on each new glyph, done with highlight colour (no layout) and drying in about 300ms.
2. **Ink colour that tells you where text lives:** fresh ink for local only, dried ink once synced, a cobalt edge on text sent to a provider, and vermilion for published.
3. **Reading-progress presence for AI editors:** a quiet marker moving through the paragraphs each editor has read, with spline smoothing, instead of a shimmer or spinner.
4. **The rubric stamp:** a short ink-impression stamp with a halftone or mis-registration shader on a small canvas. It can be dragged and reversed until a threshold, and is fully undoable.
5. **"Send to the room" as a visible delayed commit:** the envelope sits on the desk for N seconds, and you can pull it back.
6. **Out-of-credits as an empty inkwell:** the control stays focusable and says why and when the credits refill.
7. **Margin notes that slide in from the margin edge,** grouped, with a stagger of 50ms or less. They never shift the manuscript layout.
8. **Paper grain lit by the time of day:** one cached texture plus a low-resolution light pass that only re-renders when the light changes. It pauses while you type.
9. **Destructive actions as a press imprint that deepens while held,** with a keyboard path and an undo window, rather than a modal.
10. **A Desk page where stats are set like a printer's composing stick:** movement happens only when you open the page, never during writing, and scroll effects stay out of the reading column.
